Have the Government knowledge of the fact that Col. W. H. Merritt, who purports to be secretary of the Canadian Aviation Fund, is collecting or attempting to collect money for the purchase of aeroplanes. The object of the Canadian Aviation Fund is to give help to the firing line by means of trained aviators and aeroplanes. The cost of a machine is $7,600. If the Government have knowledge of Col. W. H. Merritt's operations, have those operations their approval?

House again in Committee of Supply, Mr. Rainville in the Chair.
Cape Breton telegraph system-branch telegraph line from Washabuck wharf to McKay's Point, $420.
What is the cause of the sudden demand for assistance to the telephone system?

I do not know that there is any increased demand this year. There are items in the estimates for small extensions of the telephone system owned by the Government in different parts of the country, and there will be small expenditures at the different places named. This is simply an extension of three miles of line at this particular point. The superintendent recommended it, and that is why it is being put in.
This little extension is in my riding, and I should like to know something about it. Can the minister tell me which office it is connected with, starting from Washabuck wharf5
There is a telephone line at present from Washabuck bridge to Waslia-buck Centre. It is intended to extend this line from Washabuck Centre to McKay's Point, three miles.
Where are you going to make the terminus?
At McKay's point.
Will these be telephone or telegraph offices?
It is a telephone system.

Are the telephones used anywhere else on the system in the county of Victoria?
Mr. REI1J: They are mostly telegraph lines in that county.
Is it the policy of the Government to build telephones throughout the country, and why is the Government doing it?
The Government has a telephone system in different parts of Canada.
Why?
We have had telephones for many years in certain parts of the country, and this is simply an extension.
I suppose the system is general through all parts of Canada?

Can the hon. minister tell me what communication can be obtained by the telephone system in this county, except for those three miles, which ' are not connected with the town in any way? How will the system be connected up? The whole of the rest of the system all through the county is a Government telegraph line. It is a telegraph line from Orangedale down to Washabuck Centre. The minister tells us he is going to extend that system three miles further down the line, and it is going to be a telephone system. The lines will be no use unless they connect up with some outside system, or connect somewhere with telephones.

I understand in these districts the telephone system is used at the present time, but the tendency is to change the system, and have a telephone line instead of the telegraph, and, to my mind, that would be more advantageous. But the hon. gentleman can see that, if you have the telephone, you can get the advantage of the telegraph system by telephoning your message to the telegraph office, and asking them to forward it.

If the minister will train somebody at that place in the use of the telegraph system, until they get a telephone system established, it would be an advantage. Anybody can use the telephone, but many people cannot operate the telegraph.	-

The minister has not propel ly answered the question asked by my hon. friend from Victoria-Haliburton.
It seems to me, after looking over two or three pages of the supplementary estimates, that we are raising a pretty big question. Is the Dominion Government going to establish a telephone system all over Canada, or not? I think that question should be answered. This little transaction only involves an expenditure of $420, they have already a telegraph line to Washabuck, and they are extending a wire, to be used as a telephone wire a distance of three miles, which is not very serious, but you are establishing a principle.
I do not know much about the thing locally, but I do know there is as fine a telephone system in the province of Nova Beotia as can be found in Canada. They have some sort of a municipal system, and their rates are reasonable. Here we find five or six different instances in which the Government is going into the telephone business in the province of Nova Scotia.
I think we should have some policy laid down by the minister, in order that we may know what we .are to look forwiard to. The minister knows very well that if the Government is going into competition with the telephone company one of two things will happen, either the Government will have to buy out the telephone companies, or the companies will have to go to the wall.

This particular locality is
covered at the present time by a telegraphic system. There are no telephons. The extension we aTe now providing for is a three mile extension to a system which has been in existence for many years. As I understand it, this line is not in competition with any other telephone system in that locality. In British Columbia and in some parts of the province of Quebec where they have no privately-owned telephone systems, the Government has pro- ' vided telegraphie communication for the people. In my opinion it is necessary that those systems should be changed -as quickly as possible, for the reason that it is very difficult to get telegraph operators because of the small rate of pay. It is much easier

to get operators to handle a telephone system.

The reason I asked the question was that there are certain areas in Canada which have no communication with the outside world. If the Government proposes adopting the principle of providing telegraphic and telephonic communication in one part of the country, it is only fair that every section of our great Dominion should have the same privilege. In some of the sparsely settled parts of the riding I have the honour to represent, they have no such communication, and we have had to go down into our pockets to provide funds for the building of our own telephone lines. If those lines are going to be under Government patronage in one place, they must be under Government patronage everywhere.

There are sections of
the riding I represent which are not reached by the Bell Telephone company. I have become a member of a local organization to get telephone, communication to these people. Had I known the Government intended to launch out into new fields in the federal telephone business, I would perhaps have asked the Government to build lines to some of these places. I see one province is to be given $219,000 in the supplementary estimates for telephones. When the people of other parts of the country become aware that the Government is providing telephonic communication in some parts of the country, while they have to construct their own lines, they will be displeased, to put it mildly. Years ago, of course the situation was different. Telephones were a new thing, and there was really only one company. At the present time there are local telephone systems throughout the length and breadth of the land, and we have passed legislation at this session of the House compelling the trunk lines to give connection with the local lines under certain conditions. I do not object to reasonable expenditure to open up the country, but, as my hon. friend (Sir Sam Hughes) says, if it is to be done in one part of the country it should be done everywhere. Within 150 miles of Ottawa there is territory just as remote from telephonic and telegraphic communication as is this community in Nova Scotia.

In the province of Ontario
the Government has a telephonic system.
Where?
In the Timiskaming district.

It is along the line of
railway, probably.

No, it is not along the railway We have cables to Amherst island, and we have a telephone system in some parts of New Ontario. There are so few people in the district that it would not pay a private company to build a line.
Then, am I to understand that if we come along with our petitions we will get the lines?
No, not at all. The greater part of the older counties is well settled.
What about the parts which are not settled?	-**

The municipalities can give aid to any one who would put in private lines. Who in the world would ever build a line there in the districts around Tadous-sac or Chicoutimi? Those people are entitled to some communication with the outer world.
What about Dorchester county?
The telephone system has been there for many years.
They are putting in a new one there now.

We are dealing with this particular one now, and it has been established for many years. We are only following out the policy inaugurated several years ago, to give the people in that locality the use of this line.

Could the minister tell
me how large a place Washabuck is?

Perhaps the hon. member
who comes from that district could answer that question.
Mr. McKE'NZIE: Washabuck, which is a small corner of my constituency is about the size of North' Oxford.

North Oxford is bigger
than the whole of Nova Scotia.

There is one very objectionable feature about these items. It is that they are brought in so late in the session in the supplementary estimates and in such large amounts. If it was necessary to provide for telegraph and telephone lines, the appropriation ought to have been asked for in the main estimates. The total in the main estimates for this service

is $60,875. The Supplementary Estimates are supposed to be for the purpose of covering items that have been overlooked in the Main Estimates. It is entirely wrong to leave important matters, which might as v ell have been provided for in the Main Estimates, until the Supplementary Estimates are brought down late in the session. While in the Main Estimates we are asked to privide $60,875, we are called upon to vote in the Supplementary Estimates the very large sum of $271,000 for this service, or more than four times the total of the vote contained in the Main Estimates.
I have looked through some of these items. It is evident that it was not considered desirable to put them in the Main Estimates, because the largeness of the amounts would attract public attention and invite public criticism; or that the minister, seeing an election very near at hand, is impelled to realize the importance of putting these items in the Supplementary Estimates in order to gain popularity in the districts which will be affected. It is unfair to Parliament to ask us to vote this very large sum for . this service, distributed over three provinces, and provided for in the Supplementary Estimates.

I hardly think the hon. member is putting it fairly when he suggests that we are bringing down these Estimates so late in the session on account of an election coming on. These Supplementary Estimates have been down for some time. It has always been customary to bring down such Supplementary Estimates as are necessary during the latter part of the session.
The adjournment for a couple of months and the time we have taken over important Bills has prevented the Estimates being taken up before this. When we made up these ^Estimates we believed and intended that there should not be an election this year.
That is the Main Estimates.

The main estimates and the
supplementaries were prepared long before that. The extension of Parliament was referred to in the speech from the Throne, and these supplementary estimates were already prepared before we knew there would not be an extension of Parliament.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that we would not have had any supplementary estimates if there had been an extension granted?
I say we expected we would have had an extension of Parliament.
No, you did not expect that.

Of course we expected it, because last year the extension was granted and the reasons this year were much stronger why it should be granted. If the hon. gentleman had carried out the same policy that he pursued last year, the reasons being much stronger this year, we should have had an extension of Parliament and we would not have had an election.
If the hon. gentleman had done what he promised last year he might have had an extension.

We are going to have an election, and I am going to discuss the reason why this vote is brought down. These items are here, and I am afraid that the minister intends to force them through. This is in line with the general policy that I am protesting against under present conditions. First, the minister brought down the main estimates, and he only asked for $60,000 for all the telegraph and telephone lines in Canada. The votes were largely for repairs. But now he comes with supplementaries late in the session, and he wants between $200,000 and $300,000, and not for .repairs at all. If it were only a question of the little item of $420 that is now under discussion, I would not raise any question about it. But my hon. friend is branching out upon a great scheme of public ownership of utilities in British Columbia, the end of which no man can see. He is asking for $219,000 for the province of British Columbia in addition to $22,400 voted in the main estimates. The item in the main estimates looked all right on its face. It says:
British Columbia-mainland telegraph and telephone lines-general repairs and improvements, $22,400.
That did not look very bad, and, therefore, Parliament might say that it was necessary to vote that in order to put the service in good condition and not allow deterioration to affect it. But he comes forward now with an entirely new policy. It is not a question of repairs at all; it is an absolutely new policy as far as British Columbia is concerned. A new policy also is contemplated in so far as some portions of Nova Scotia are concerned. I am not sufficiently acquainted with the geography of that portion of Nova Scotia to know exactly whether they have a telephone system in any of these places, but they must have in many of them. I cannot conceive that there are half a dozen places in Cape

Breton island where they do not have the telephone. The conclusion is forced upon one's mind that there is some connection between these telegraph lines being converted into telephone lines and the election. I know the gentleman who manipulates affairs in Cape Breton island. His name was mentioned last night.
Mr. Douglas.

Yes, John C. Douglas, and one becomes suspicious when he sees items like these appearing in the supplementary estimates. I have no objection to the $420 being expended for extending this line three miles, but I am going to vote against this item as a matter of principle. I asked the minister to cut out a quarter of a million dollars at St. John, for which I know a great many people will not thank me, and he has done it. I asked him to cut out a quarter of a million dollars at another place, -which the minister has agreed to do. Now he comes forward with a quarter of a million for telegraph and telephone lines in British Columbia, and I am going to vote against it because I think it is my duty to do so.
I take the ground on broad principles that if everybody is asked to retrench owing to the exigencies of the situation, surely the Government ought to be asked to retrench. They have given us their pledge that they will not embark on any new schemes, and if they cannot build wharves, breakwaters or railroads, surely they are not justified in going on with a great system of telephones, the end of which nobody can see. I am voting against it on that broad ground. I quite agree with the minister that if you have a telegraph line and want to make a short extension it may be better to instal the telephone rather than the telegraph. That is quite reasonable. I know there was a time when it was necessary that the federal Government should extend the telephone line to the Yukon, as private enterprise could not do it. The Government was equally justified in building telegraph lines down the St. Lawrence and into the Saguenay and Chicoutimi districts. Private enterprise would not build up the Saguenay twenty-five years ago, and a line was necessary in order to give those people an outlet. It may have been necessary to build a telegraph line in Cape Breton island, although I do not believe it. But, I do not think it is necessary that this Government should vote $10,000 or $12,000 to extend that system in Cape [DOT] Breton island, or $2,400 for a line in '
the county of Quebec. And surely it is not necessary to spend $2,500 for a telephone line in Dorchester. I am not now saying anything about British Columbia. The whole thing is as plain as the nose on a man's face the Government are starting out for the election and certain men have got in their work and have had these items put in the estimates. I think the Government should drop all these votes.

Whgn the Government established the telegraph line in Cape Breton, that course was quite justified, but when it comes to establishing telephones in the province of Nova Scotia, that is quite different. The provincial government some years ago passed an Act providing for the incorporation of rural* telephone companies. The provincial government gave aid to these companies sufficient to pay for the wires and insulators, and for the swinging of the wires, so that the shareholders are called upon only to furnish the poles and set them up. As a consequence of that policy we have many rural telephone companies in Nova Scotia and they give a very efficient service. Their systems are connected, under the authority of the Utilities Board at Halifax, with the main telephone system of Nova Scotia. If the Government embark on a system of establishing telephone lines, they will interfere very materially with the enterprise of the people of Nova Scotia, which has already developed a very important system of rural telephones. If the Government contemplated only the extension of the telegraph lines, particularly for short distances like three miles, there could be no real objection, but I do say they are going to interfere with the enterprise and the industry of the people of eastern Nova Scotia and the island of Cape Breton if they establish a system of telephones. We will then have a multiplicity of telephone systems that will only lead to confusion and add to the cost to those who are obliged to use the telephone lines. The subscribers to rural telephone Companies have to pay for their connection with the main telephone system, and if the Government establish a system of their own it means additional tolls to the subscribers, and more evil than good will result from the action of the Government. I do say that at present, in view of the assistance given to the establishing of rural telephone lines in Nova Scotia, this Government is going out of its way to interfere with a development that should be left entirely to the people.
I propose to move an amendment which I think is in order. I have not it written, but perhaps the minister would consent to its being passed.
Who is the general superintendent of Government telephone and telegraph lines in Cape Breton?
The deputy tells me he thinks his name is McKee.
Tihat is the general superintendent at St. John. He is the manager of the Western Union. There is a man, .1 think, named Livingstone.
He is a line repairer under Mr. McKee.
He has general charge of all lines in Cape Breton.

Under Mr. McKee.
Mr. KYTE. Then there is a local man in each county responsible for the making of repairs. Who is responsible for seeing that these assistants actually do their work?
Of course the system follows down from the general superintendent to each individual officer.
If an assistant repairer was not doing his work, it would be the general repairer who would report to the Government.

He would report to his
superior officer.

Who would see that a man who was not doing his duty was dismissed. I have a case in my county where that practice was not followed. I shall read the correspondence, which was produced in the House a few days ago, in answer to an order for all correspondence etc., relating to the dismissal of Hector Urquhart, as linemen between Grand river and Enon, Cape Breton county, and the appointment of Dan A. McLennan in his place. The correspondence reads:
Glace Bay, C.B., Sept. 16, 1916. Hon. Robert Rogers,
Minister of Public Works,
Ottawa.
Re Government Telegraphs.
Dear Mr. Minister:-
I hereby recommend the dismissal of Hector Urquhart of Grand river, Richmond county, as telegraph line repairman, and the appointment of Dan A. McLennan, Head of Loch Lomond, as his successor.
The new appointee is more suitably located for giving attention to the repair work on the line, besides he is more efficient.
Yours faithfully,
(Sgd.) Jno. C. Douglas.
Telegraph Service, P.W.D.,
Ottawa, Sept, 27, 1916.
John C. Douglas, Esq.,
Glace Bay, N.S.
Local Repairer, Grand river-Enon.
Dear Sir:-
Having reference to your letter of the 16th instant to the Hon. the Minister of Public Works, I beg to acquaint you that an authorization has been given for the discontinuance of the services of Mr. Hector Urquhart and the appointment of Mr. Dan A. McLennan, Head of Lock Lomond, to succeed him.
The arrangement is being put into effect forthwith.
Yours faithfully,
(Sgd.) D. H. Keeley, General Superintendent.
Then there are the following letters:
Ottawa, Sept. 27, 1916. Hector Urquhart, Esq.,
Grand river, C.B.
Dear Sir:
I have from the Hon. the Minister of Public Works an instruction to discontinue your services as local repairer for the telegraph line between Grand river and Enon. You might please deliver to our agent at Grand river the tools, etc., which you have in your charge. The superintendent at St. John, Mr. C. W. McKee, is being advised of this requirement and will send you in due course whatever -payment is due to you to the end of the present month.
Yours faithfully,
(Sgd.) D. H. Keeley,
Gen.-Supt.
Ottawa, Sept. 27, *1916. Dan. A. McLennan, Esq.,
Head of Loch Lomond, C.B.
Dear Siv:
I have from the Hon. the Minister of Public Works an authorization given on the recom mendation of Mr. J. C. Douglas for your appointment as local repairer for the Government telegraph lines between Grand river and Enon, a distance of about 19 J miles. The pay attached to this position is fifty dollars ($50) per annum, without any other allowance, and you will be expected to keep the line clear of interruption and promptly make trips over it for that purpose whenever called upon to do so by the Superintendent, Mr. C. W. McKee, at St. John, N.B., or his representative, Mr. A E. Hoyt at North Sydney. Anything in the way of overhauling or reconstruction work when required will be attended by the general repairer for the district. The tools, etc., which have been in the care of the former repairer are being turned over to our agent at Grand river to whom you might please apply for them. Mr. McKee is being? advised of your appointment, please let him know when you are ready and the payment for your ser-



vices will begin from the date you enter upon your duties.
Tours faithfully,
(Sgd.) D. H. Keeley,
Gen.-Supt.
Ottawa, Sept. 27, 1916.
C.	W. McKee, Esq.,
Supt. Govt. Telegraph Service,
St. John, N.B.
Dear Sir:-Local Repairer-Grand River

Enon.
A change in the above position has heeti ordered whereby Mr. Hector Urquhart is to be retired and will be succeeded by Mr. Dan. A. McLennan of Head of Loch Lomond.
You might please see what it is contained in the two accompanying copies of letters sent to Messrs. Urquhart and McLennan to-day and take such further action as is found to be called for.
Tours faithfully,
(Sgd.) D. H. Keeley,
Gen.-Supt.
That is the history of this extraordinary transaction. The facts are these:	Mr. E.
D.	McKillop who had the Government telegraph office at Grand River falls, and whose wife was the telegraph operator removed from that district about a year ago.	The	telegraph	office,	therefore,became vacant. Two applicants for the position presented themselves. One was this man D. A. McLennan and the other was	a man	named	McLeod.
They were equally deserving in the eyes of Mr. John C. Douglas, who holds the patronage -for the county of Richmond. Mr. Douglas was unable to give both the position of telegraph operator, so he decided that he would have Mr. Hector Urquhart dismissed from the trifling position which be held as assistant to the repairer at. St. Peter's, and bestow the position upon Mr. Dan A. McLennan. Through the adoption of this course, both his supporters would be reconciled; both would get some consideration for their political services. The minister said that the general repairer would be responsible to the Government for the proper discharge of the duties of the assistant repairers. That would appear to be reasonable and proper. If Mr. Hector Urquhart was not properly discharging the duties of his position, one would imagine that this Government would have received a report back from the local superintendent of lines to Mr. McKee at St. John, which report would have been transmitted to the department. No such thing happened ; there was no question whatever about the efficiency with which Mr. 
Urquhart was discharging his 4 p.m. duties. He bad been assistant to the repairer for seven or eight years; no complaints had ever been made. If any complaints were to be made on account of any deficiency on his part, those complaints . would come through the repairer at St. Peter's. But, upon the recommendation of Mr. John C. Douglas, the dispenser of patronage in that part of the country, who asserted that Mr. Hector Urquhart was not efficiently discharging his duties, the Government, without obtaining any report from their own officials, discharged Mr. Urqu-hart from the position which he held and handed over his paltry salary of $50 to Mr. Dan. A. McLennan, solely because of the dispute which had arisen as to which applicant should receive the position in the telegraph office. I am glad to see the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) in his place, because the noble sentiments that he expressed two years ago, in which he deprecated the idea that patronage should continue, still re-echo through this Chamber. Only two days ago, when the member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) suggested that -there might be patronage in connection with the appointment of a commission that was under discussion at that time, the minister indignantly repudiated the idea that such would be the case. It is a matter of regret that the principles adhered to by the Minister of Trade and Commerce have not been adopted by his colleagues in the Cabinet. We have here the most contemptible instance of political partisanship ever heard of in a county where many instances have occurred in the last four or five years. Appeals are being made to all classes of the community to make sacrifices on account of the conditions in which we	find	ourselves;	appealsare being	made to all	political
parties to forget politics, to get together, to form a union government, to devote all their energies towards carrying on the war. While these professions of a desire for union among the people are being made, cabinet ministers resort to the most contemptible means of persecution of those who are not of the same political faith as themselves. I realize that nothing we can say on this side of the House will change the temper and spirit of the Government or the principles upon which it acts, but .it is well that while these professions are being made by gentlemen upon the Government benches and by those sitting behind them; while they assert that they have eliminated politics entirely from all considerations of govern

ment, and that they honestly desire all political parties to unite for the purpose of carrying on the war, it is well that these instances should be brought before the public in order to show the people how hollow is the hypocrisy practised by lion, gentlemen opposite.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Kyte) is very much exercised over the fact that the late Minister of Public Works (Hon. Robert Rogers) took some advice from Mr. John C. Douglas. This is not the first time the hon. member has brought the name of Mr. John C. Douglas before the House. Every session an attack is made upon Mr. Douglas. My only knowledge of Mr. Douglas is that obtained through his visits to Ottawa, but I have always found him an upright and honourable man. I do not think that I am the only one who has confidence in Mr. Douglas. He placed himself before the constituents of the district which my hon. friend represents, or a portion of it, and if I remember rightly, he carried the constituency by an overwhelming majority. The people in that district, therefore, hold Mr. Douglas in great esteem; they showed by their vote that they preferred him to the gentleman who opposed him. Simply because Mr. Douglas places before the Government at Ottawa the requests of the people whom he has the honour to represent, is he to be slandered by the hon. gentleman? Is it to be said that the only way the people of my hon. friend's constituency can get fair play is by the adoption of his recommendations? With all due respect to the hon. member, if the patronage of his constituency were left in his hands, I would say: God help the Conservatives in that district.
That is my opinion of the hon. member. I am not saying it unfairly. I believe the hon. member has so much sympathy for his own friends that he would supply them first with all that they could get, and after that there would 'be nothing left for the Conservatives. The hon. member has also stated that this Government has been preaching that, since they have been in power, they have been treating those of the opposite political faith fairly. That is a fact. We have been dealing fairly with and keeping on all the officials, unless, by their own actions, they are entitled to be dismissed. I say, with all frankness, that that has been the case, and it is unfair for the hon. member to make such statements so far as public officials are concerned. Officials in both the Inside and Outside Ser-
340i
vices would justify the statement I have just made. The hon. member, because some officials have been dismissed on account of actions of their own, makes this onslaught to-day. Mr. John C. Douglas represents this particular constituency in the local legislature.
He does not represent this constituency.
He represents a constituency in the local legislature.
The adjoining one.

Well, the adjoining one. He has made the statement that he believes the people of that district would be better served if the office was more conveniently situated. The Great Northwestern Telegraph company, or the' Canadian Pacific Railway company, change their offices every day in towns, villages, and districts to suit the convenience of the people of these localities. Just because Mr. Douglas happens to be the local member, a Conservative, and because the people of that district have done him the honour to choose him as a candidate at the next election to oppose some one-I do not know whether it is the hon. member or not-the hon. niem-ber makes this onslaught. I believe the representations of Mr. Douglas are entitled to consideration, and I do not believe he deserves the remarks made by the hon. member.

The minister entirely loses the point of my criticism. I have no fault to find with the Government accepting political recommendations from Mr. John C. Douglas, as he is in charge of the patronage of that district. That, however, is not the case in this instance. Mr. John C. Douglas states that Mr. Urquhart is inefficient, that he ought to be dismissed for inefficiency, and another man appointed. What I find fault with is that there is no report from Mr. Urquhart's superior officer as to the manner in which he has been carrying on his work. If Mr. Douglas had said that Mr. Urquhart was a political partisan, and that, therefore, he ought to be dismissed, then on account of the precedents established by this Government during the last four or five years, nobody would be surprised, that his recommendation should be carried out, but he could not say that about Mr. Urquhart.

Did not Mr. Douglas recommend this change in the location of the

office in order that the people might be better served?
Is not the man placed over Mr. Urquhart the proper person to make a report to the department on that point?

He may state that this man is well qualified to discharge his duties, but he cannot state as to- the suitability of the location of the office. The people in the surrounding district would know what is most convenient for them.

The general repairer for the telegraph lines lives at St. Peter's and goes over that territory week after week. He has on the line two or three assistants who have been there for the last five or six years. If Mr. Urquhart is not suitably situated to discharge his duties, or if he is inefficient, one would imagine that the Government would have received a report from Mr. Urquhart's superior officer, that report transmitted, if you will, by Mr. Douglas to the department. There is no suggestion from the general repairer for that district that Mr. Urquhart is inefficient or that he is not suitably located. Mr. Douglas wanted the office for a political friend. He could not trump up a charge of political partisanship against Mr. Urquhart, so he wrote a letter to the minister containing this statement:
The new appointee is more suitably located tor giving attention to the repair work on the line, besides he is more efficient.
One would imagine that the minister _ would have transmitted Mr. Douglas' let" ter to Mr. McKee, the superintendent over that section of the telegraph line, and got a report from him. Nothing whatever was done in that direction. Mr. Douglas' unsupported statement that Mr. Urquhart was inefficient in the discharge of his duties was accepted by the minister, and his dismissal was immediately asked for. The minister expressed a pious hope that God might help the Conservative party. If that is the best example that can be given of defence for their conduct, then I say: God help the Conservative party in the hands of the minister.

We are lectured almost out of sight this afternoon because we happened to mention the name of this saintly, man, John C. Douglas. If the minister will listen to me for a moment, he will understand why we do not like the idea of a government led and directed * by Mr. John C. Douglas. Mr. Douglas is the local member for the county of Cape Bre-

ton, and if the minister would follow his history and the ways by which he succeeded in creating certain dissensions in the mining communities, so that he managed to secure a majority, he would not be very proud that this gentleman represents the county of Cape Breton. I had the privilege of meeting Mr. John C. Douglas in a local contest in the county of Victoria. He had in his hand a telegram which he said was from the Minister of Railways (Mr. Cochrane) telling him that a Mr. Angus R. Campbell, who had been dismissed by the Minister of Railways from the West Bay Road station on the Intercolonial would be restored to his position in a very short time. The telegram arrived in the county while the contest was on and while I was there with Mr. Douglas. Knowing the Minister of Railways, I was very much surprised that he would send such a telegram. I did not believe he had done so; I told the people I did not believe it; but Mr. Douglas was the big man that he is in the estimation of the Minister of Customs and acting Minister of Public Works, and people around there believed that he had received that telegram from the Minister of Railways. ' Mr. Douglas fooled this poor fellow who was dismissed and his friends into voting for his party. The man who was elected in the contest was unseated on account of bribery and corruption. Mr. Douglas went on the stand at the trial; the copy of this telegram was produced to him, and he was asked on oath: " Did you get this telegram from Mr. Cochrane?" He said:	"Yes, not only did I get the telegram from Mr. Cochrane, but I discussed the matter with Mr. Cochrane." Shortly afterwards I moved in this House for all the correspondence and papers .passed between the Minister of Railways and* Mr. Douglas. Papers were brought down, and the return is still obtainable in this House, but there was never such a telegram sent. To make sure, I went to the minister and said: "Surely Mr. Douglas would not first lie .about this thing to me and then go on the stand and. swear to it." I asked the minister if there was such a telegram, and be told me that he never bad, at least up to that date, had the slightest communication of any kind, by telegram or otherwise, with this man Douglas.
Still he went lying -around the country, representing that Mr. Cochrane was trying to interfere in a local election. Mr. Campbell was never restored, and the minister never promised to restore him, but he got a few votes on the strength of ttfe state-

ment. He got into the box and swore that a thing, which never existed, was true. That is the character of man the minister has in Mr. Douglas. His name is like a red rag to gentlemen who want to do things in a decent and honest way. If the minister desires to be led by John C. Douglas, he will have lots of trouble. I am simply giving a small part of his character.

Is the minister not going to consider the question whether he should pass these estimates for telegraph lines? I see no reason why telegraph lines should be built in Cape Breton, and not in other parts of Nova Scotia. It has been drawn to the minister's attention already that we have a very good telephone system in that province, and there are scarcely any of the rural districts which are not now supplied with telephones. The local government has done a great deal to encourage the telephone system of the province. They have a superintendent who looks over the ground when any new line is to be established, and the government gives financial assistance, and the farmers and fishermen can, without expense get incorporation to organize telephone companies. There is a subsidy of $20 a mile which, as the hon. gentleman from Richmond stated, in ordinary times paid for the wire, so that the local people have only to provide the poles, and set them up, and provide the boxes which is done at very little expense. In this way provincial government aid has enabled the people of Nova Scotia to have rural telephones in all the districts. Unless we are going to embark on a Federal Government telephone system, and supply such places as Mabou harbour. Margaree harbour and Baddeck with telephones, I do not understand what justification there can be for this vote. There must be something behind this that we do not understand. No one from that locality will tell the minister that it is necessary to spend this public money in that district, unless it is for the accommodation of one or two friends of John C. Douglas. No doubt it is a political scheme, and I do not think the minister should ask the House, at a time like this when we are endeavouring to save money, to embark on the work of constructing these lines, unless the minister agrees to . embark generally on the construction of telephone lines. We should, not start this construction unless we adopt some kind of a policy on the whole question. The minister is projecting not only
these lines in, Nova Scotia, but lines in the other provinces of Canada, which we find provided for in these estimates. If we pass this item for the construction of telephone lines in Novia Scotia without any protest, we will be committed to the construction of telephone lines in other provinces. We want to know what the minister's policy is. Is he going to build telephone lines all through Canada, or is he not? If he is not,
I do not think these lines proposed in Nova Scotia are justified a.t all.

In Cape Breton we have, on the Government system, 948 miles of lines, of which 719 are operated by telephone, with 88 offices, and 129 operated by telegraph, with 45 offices. This system has 'been established for years.
I am talking about extensions.

This is for half a dozen extensions. It is not a new policy. $3,400 of this item is for re-poling and general repairs. Every year since the system was started small extensions have 'been made. Whether it is a government or a private system, small extensions will always be necessary. [DOT]
Will the minister establish telephone lines in my constituency if I send a list of those that are necessary?

None of these systems are on the mainland, which is served by a private corporation. If we acceded to the hon. gentleman's request we would be starting on a new policy, so far as the mainland of Nova Scotia is concerned, and that question would have to be considered 'before I could give an answer.
Are not those lines in British Columbia and the other provinces on the mainland?

They are in outside districts, which are sparsely settled, and where you , could not get a private corporation to build a telephone system. Those systems were established years ago. We had them in the Yukon long ago-.

I see here an item for a branch telephone line from Inverness to Mabou harbour. There as two possible routes which that line might follow. I want to know which route it will follow. I am quite in accord with the idea of constructing that branch, because it is very necessary. I have been advocating it for years.
That is from Inverness to Sight point, Sight point to Mahon mines, and Mabou mines to Mabou harbour.
What is the distance?

Five miles from Inverness to Port Ban, and two and one half miles from Port Ban to Sight point, seven miles from-Sight point to Mabou Mines, and three miles from Mabou mines to Mabou harbour; a total of seventeen and one-half miles.

This line goes from
Margaree harbour to Chimney comer. How is it that this line stops at Chimney corner contrary to the promise made to me six months ago? I cannot understand why the line should be stopped there, because that is only a short distance from Margaree harbour, and just as important a section of the country lies to the south of that. 1 would expect the line to go at least as far as Ste. Rose and Dunvegan to serve the whole settlement there. I have been advocating this for the last two years and got the assurance of the Government that the line would extend from Margaree to Dun-vegan. I think the line should stop at Dun-vegan. I am not finding fault with this construction, because it is only in accord with the suggestions I have been making for two years and the Government is only carrying out part of their promise. The only fault I find is that they are not carrying the line as far as they promised.
I understand the hon. gentleman thinks that this line running from Margaree harbour to .Chimney corner, five miles,.should be continued six miles further.
I should think it should go six miles further, because there is a very important settlement there all along the line to Dunvegan.

The proposal of the minister this year is to take the five miles and in another year he will consider the extension. These are all small extensions, and there are requests for further extensions. They must be extended to these different places from time to time as the Government can see its way clear to extend them. That has been the policy of all governments for the last thirty or forty years in regard to these telephone and telegraph systems. The hon. member knows that members on both sides of this House from those different places which are dependent on telephone and telegraph lines owned by the Govern-

ment have asked for these things, and this is part of what has been asked for.

There is only one complaint I have to make, and it is the same as the complaint I made last year. So far as the county of Inverness is concerned, the policy is not an old one at all. It was inaugurated by the present Government in 1911. The late Government had provided for telegraph lines in certain sections of the county, which were in process of completion when the present Government took charge. This Government converted, the telegraph system into a telephone system. I cannot understand why the Department of Public Works would not extend the same privilege to our people as would be extended to them by any private telephone corporation. For instance, if John Smith, or Tom Jones, wishes to get a telephone in his house he should be able to do so. The Government will not permit this, however. I cannot understand why they insist on placing the telephone offices in the hands of their own friends, to the exclusion of every one else. I submitted this complaint to the Minister of Public Works last year. If it is the intention of the Government to serve the public, I cannot see any reason why they should refuse telephones to any person who is prepared to pay for them. I know the system as it is now is nothing more nor less than a little bit of political machinery. I have no doubt if my own party came into power, and if we were to allow certain advisers to guide us, the same system would be followed. Personally, 1 would not stand for it, and the best element of the population would not stand for it. To my mind it is a preposterous condition of affairs that you cannot go to any of these telephones and talk to your friends without everybody excepting your friends hearing what you have to say.
Does the minister want any further evidence of the absolute viciousness of the whole system, beyond what has been given by the hon. member for Inverness?
The hon. member has just said he requested this line.

Think of a telephone
system being installed for the benefit of the public, and a Liberal cannot get a telephone in his house even if he is willing to pay for it, and cannot hold a conversation over the telephone without every Conservative in the place hearing what he has to say. The minister wants Parliament to

vote nearly $300,000 to perpetuate a system of that kind. Of course, the minister is not responsible for this condition of affairs, and I sympathize with him. He is working under an existing system, and he is forced to ooane here and put this through. At the same time, any man who. has any idea of right and wrong must rebel against the perpetration of such a system. If you are going to run a telephone line for the benefit of the public why cannot every man get an instrument if he is willing to pay for it and comply with the requirements? I am a director of the 'New Brunswick Telephone company, and I can speak with some knowledge of the business. If any officer of our company refused to instal an instrument, for a man who was prepared to pay for it and to comply with the requirements, such an officer would not last ten minutes. Just as long as this Government, or I think any other government in Canada, tries to operate telephones, or railways, or electric lights, or any other public service in Canada, just so long will you have this contemptible, small, party patronage. It seems to- me the time has come when the Government should be big enough to get away from this. I am not taking any " holier than thou attitude," and I admit if our party came into power many people would wish to perpetuate the same contemptible little system. It seems to me there must be a great change of sentiment in Canada before any Government can carry on these systems and make them of any practical benefit to the public. The whole principle is so vicious that I feel the minister would be justified in abandoning it entirely, not only in Nova Scotia, but in Dorchester county and everywhere else, and when the war is over let us see if we cannot get back to some sort of business principles. If the Government is going to operate telephones, let it make some arrangement with the local people to go out of business, then take over the lines and give a really useful and businesslike service. There must be many places in the island of Cape Breton where they have telephone communication at the present time? Are there no. telephone systems in Inverness?
Yes, but not sufficient. We want to get more.

The heading of this item is somewhat misleading. I asked the minister if this little extension from Washabuck Wharf to McKay's point was a telegraph line or a telephone line, and the minister told me it was a telephone line. If it is a
telegraph line I have no fault to find, because it is a continuation of the line which is there already.
The deputy minister informed me it was a telephone line, but that is a mistake. It is a telegraph line, and it is so marked on the map.
That is certainly sensible, because it is a continuation of a telegraph line already in existence.

What are the rules and regulations governing the location of instruments, the granting of privileges, the tolls or rentals, the revenue received, and the operating expenses? I would like the minister to tell us just how bad it ft, from an economic standpoint.
The information my hon. friend is asking for is published.
What is the deficit?
I do not know what the deficit is. We have quite a telegraph and telephone system in Canada, comprising about 11,600 miles altogether.
How many instruments have you?

I could not say offhand. Of course, you cannot expect much of a revenue from many of these places. It costs a great deal of money to build a line, and in many sections the country is sparsely settled. My hon. friend may be right in saying that probably the time is coming when this whole system should be revised, but it is a system which has grown up, and these extensions have to be made. I do not see that we can do anything else, unless we took over the whole thing.

I will admit that so far as Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and possibly Ontario lines are concerned, the system may not be so reprehensible, because there you are to some extent face to face with existing conditions. Quebec and British Columbia are different, and I have some doubt as to the advisability-
There are none in Ontario.

Yes, I find this item in the estimates.
Bath, Amherst Island telephone line-reconstruction and improvement, $2,200.
There is one part of my question to which the minister has not replied, and that is: What are the conditions of the service?

How do people obtain instruments and what rentals or tolls are charged? We all have some idea what it is costing for telephone service generally and I would like to know what people are - paying for this service. I would like also to know if what my hon. friend from Inverness (Mr. Chisholm) says is correct. If it be true that nobody can get telephones, except a few picked out by the patronage committees for the purpose of listening to all that is going over the line, there would not be much business done over a line of that kind.

I heard the remark of the hon. member for Inverness and it strikes me that it would be a remarkable system if it wtts carried on in that way and if it is being carried on in that way, it will be remedied. It would not be fair to have a system that only those who might be supporting the political party in power would be allowed to use, and conversations were permitted to be publicly known. With reference to the other question as to the conditions under which the telephone and telgraph services are given to the public, I might say that we have 10,300 miles of telegraph lines. There is only one office and one operator in each locality. There are 1,300 miles of telephone lines throughout Canada. My information is that people living along the line are entitled to telephones on payment of a rental. The rental varies in different localities. There is no regular rate. It just depends on the different settlements.
Does the minister mean to say that they have no schedule by which a man can say: "I am entitled to a telephone if I pay so much a year"?
It differs in different localities.

How could it differ? If you have a telephone line in Cape Breton, does the minister mean to say there is no schedule by which a man can shy: "If I pay a rental of $15, or $18, or $21 a year, I can get an instrument"? Is it as bad as that? If it is, it is worse than the condition pointed out by my hon. friend from Inverness, because in my friend's case the use of this service is confined to one political party. If on the other hand, there is no schedule and they can give one friend a telephone for $10 and the next one a telephone for $15, the minister is discriminating as between his own friends.

My information is that the
rates vary. The rate in one locality may

be more than it is in another. When a telephone line is constructed in Inverness or any other locality, the Government w'ill charge a rental that will pay for the maintenance and cost of construction of the line. They are not making a lot of money out of it. They want to give the people the benefit of this service at the lowest rate. In some localities the line may cost more than in others. It is not like a private corporation that is in it to make profits.
As much as the public utility boards will allow them.

They may possibly do that
in New Brunswick.
That is done in Ontario too.

In Ontario the service is
pretty good, but there are some parts of Canada where it is not as good as in Ontario or New Brunswick. That is the reason why the rates vary.
What is the rate in Cape Breton?
I have not got it before me.

The minister ought
to have that information.
I will get it.

All we ever heard about this telegraph service in Cape Breton was in connection with the Victoria by-election. It was used by the Conservative party to carry messages free for the Conservative party prior to the election. It was thrown absolutely open. They sent as many messages as they pleased to people along the line and paid nothing for the service. It was proven at the trial that any messages sent by tne -other side were open to them and that there was no secrecy about the messages. That seems to bear out the theory of my hon. friend from Inverness (Mr. Chisholm) that this telegraph and telephone system is just an annex to the patronage committee of the Conservative party in Cape Breton. That is one reason why we would like to have more information. I would like the minister to tell the committee if these lines are free to the Conservative party in Cape Breton and, if he is charging anything to others, what amount is he charging. My hon. friend from Inverness has made the statement that the department does not give accommodation to people along the line if they are not of the right political stripe. That is rather a serious charge.

I do not want to vote for this appropriation, although it is small, unless the minister will say that	every
man along tihe line, of whatever stripe of politics he may be, will be entitled to hook on the line provided he pays for it at a uniform rate. My hon. friend from Inverness has stated that he had complained last year that people who had made application had been unable to get the telephone service while the country is paying for the lines. Will the minister say that in future any man who applies for a telephone, lives up to the rules, whatever they are, and pays his money, will be entitled to the service?

I will certainly say that. If the telephone service is there, every man, irrespective of what his politics are, must have a telephone in accordance with the rules that have been laid down for that particular line. I will find out if there are any complaints and, if there are, they will be attended to. I have sent for the rates. This line has been there for many years. I suppose that while my hon. friends opposite were in power for fifteen or sixteen years the line was carried on.
No, the telephone has been in existence only for the last five years.
That is only in that constituency, but there are other parts where it must have been for a longer period.
That was the telegraph line.

If there has been any change in the telegraph or telephone system, or if the limes are being used as the hon. member has said, that would be most unfair and unjust, and I do not think any minister would stand for it for a minute, or permit any operator in charge of an office to be guilty of such conduct.
Are there not public pay stations with cabinets?
There are public pay stations into which any person can go and talk so that the operator cannot hear.
Then how does the want of secrecy occur?
They have their public places to talk.
No.
No. There is no such thing on Cape Breton Island as a pay station with a cabinet. The telephone instrument is put into the kitchen of somebody who happens to be the head worker for the party.
The hon. gentleman does not know, he has not been there himself.

I am properly describing the conditions. I have been in Cape Breton island a good many times, and I know something about what goes on down there. Talking about having a cabinet with any secrecy in a public telephone system on the island of Cape Breton-you might as well talk about finding a white blackbird. They do not do it that way.
That is true of some other telephone systems is it not?
To some extent.
People are very curious.

But in other places they make a pretense of secrecy. Not so in Cape Breton Island. Does the department rent telephones to subscribers or simply put an instrument in some person's house and call that a station from which the people may telephone? I had an idea that there was no such thing there as rental to subscribers. People simply use sufficient political influence to have a telephone put in somebody's kitchen and then the neighbours go and talk over the instrument in the kitchen while the family carry on their conversation.
It cannot be that way unless it is a thing inherited in 1911 by my hon. friend.
There were no telephones then, they were all telegraphs.

These listening boards seem to have been established since 1911. I want to ask the minister if he thinks it right, under present conditions, to put in the estimates $272,000 for telephone in British Columbia?
That is not all for telephones, seme of it is for repairs to present lines.

There is $272,000 for telephone and telegraph systems, and a great portion of that is for new lines. For repairs to existing lines, provision should be made, because otherwise these lines would go out of use, and the people who now have the accommodation should not be deprived of it; we should keep up our property. But when the minister starts out on

the wholesale construction of new lines, it is not fair to the country. Of this $272,000, I imagine $50,000 or $60,000 would repair all his lines, and to that extent no person could object to the vote. But the people of Canada, in their present temper, with our taxation and the financial pressure now upon us, no matter what their politics may be, will wonder how the Government can justify the plunging into an expenditure of more than a quarter of a million dollars where perhaps $50,000 or $60,000 would do. Every person is making some sacrifice, and if the people who will be accommodated by this large new expenditure were asked, I have no doubt that 95 per cent of them would say: Let it stand until after the war is over. That is the spirit of the Canadian people. We heard this afternoon about a request made by Lieutenant-Colonel Merritt. We have all received that request. One of the great needs of the Allies to-day is greater strength in the air. We read to-day, yesterday, and the day before, of attacks made on London and other parts of England by air raiders. Colonel Merritt asks that a large number of air fighting machines be procured, and so necessary does he think they are that he is soliciting private aid. With this vote of $272,000, thirty-eight air fighting machines could be procured. If we took $60,000 out of this $272,000 for repairs, and I submit that would be enough, we could send the Allies thirty of these air fighting machines. I leave it to the minister to say to which purpose we ought to devote this money.

I am not surprised that the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) should oppose publie ownership. I understand that he is a director and shareholder in a very profitable electric light company and also in a very profitable telephone company, a privately owned corporation; and it is not uncommon for men in those positions to resist any advance along the line of public ownership. But if I have observed the attitude of the public correctly, the whole trend is towards the public ownership- of these public utilities, and although these big financiers, who are looking for big profits, may resist and protest, this wave of public ownership is coming over this country. The hon. member for Carleton and all the other vested interests in the country notwithstanding, public ownership is going to prevail in this country, and the people are going to be served well.

That is the first time
I was ever called a big financier. I do not rMr. Graham.]
know whether to take that as complimentary or otherwise.

I think my hon. friend is fast approaching that class, and if his company is allowed to operate these concerns, which I believe are very successful, he will approach that class, if he is not in it already.
I am a little surprised that hon. gentlemen representing Nova Scotia constituencies have not arisen to defend the maintenance by the Government of telephone and telegraph lines in Cape Breton. I am not particularly acquainted with the locality but I have been there several times, and my observation has been that the telephone and telegraph services there are of great convenience to the people. I refer particularly to North Cape Breton -and Victoria. There are in that county large sections where the people are very much isolated and would be almost out of the world if they were not kept in touch with other parts of the province by means of the telegraph. Without it they would never get news or be able to summon a doctor, as no private company would think of establishing a telephone or telegraph line there for profit. Such a line must be run at a loss. But the people are a deserving people; they are doing a good work; they are engaged in fishing and producing wealth for the country, and I think it is only just that- the Government should spend money in their behalf.
I should be sorry if the Government curtailed a public service of- this kind. I was amazed at the assertion made by the -member for Inverness (Mr. Chisholm) in regard to the partisan manner in which, as he alleges, the system i.s conducted. I would not doubt the word of my hon. friend;
I do not believe that he would deliberately deceive the people, but I am inclined to think that he has been victimized; he has been wrongly informed. I should be surprised, indeed, if, in a certain village where there was a telephone line, a man would be refused a telephone because he was a Liberal and another man would be given one because he was a Conservative.
It was a surprise to me.

I would like the hon. gentleman to give the chapter and verse;
I would like him to give the names. The hon. gentleman would not dare go into the county of Inverness and make the statements that he has made here to-day.
I do not believe that anything of the kind

is done. It is true that a man living remote from the main line might make application for a telephone and the authorities, upon consideration, might decide that it was not practicable to grant his request. But that is what private corporations are doing. The company of the member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) does not put in at the regular rate a telephone for every person who asks for it; it does not run private wires six or seven miles for the sake of giving service to one person. So that quite as much complaint could be made about the operation of telephones and telegraphs by private corporations in Nova Scotia as could be made respecting the operation of lines by the Government. The hon. gentleman speaks about the lack of a public telephone. In every rural community in Nova Scotia the same method is followed as that which is followed by the Government in Cape Breton county. Perhaps in a certain locality a public telephone will be placed in somebody's kitchen. A man comes in and uses the phone; somebody on the line may hear his message. But you cannot expect in a rural community all the facilities and accommodations that are afforded in cities. The Government telephones are operated in Nova Scotia just as other privately owned telephone systems are operated under similar circumstances. There is a regular scale of rates; the public are served much in the same way, but with this difference: the private corporation could not be induced to serve some of the territories that are served by Government telephone systems. Through the extension of the (government phones to these remote districts, great convenience is 5 p.m. enjoyed by the people. I think the people would resent the suggestion that the Government should withdraw from this business and allow privately owned and operated telephone systems to serve the country. So far from suggesting that government ownership of telephones be curtailed, I would say that we ought to enlarge and extend the operation of such government owned public utilities.

I do not know why my hon. friend is so lavish with his challenges. He does not know the first thing about the matter; he does not know any more about the district that I have in mind than a babe unborn.
May I ask the hon. gentleman to be good enough to give the names and the places where, as he states, such discrimination occurred?

I wish the hon. gentleman would be good enough to sit down until I have finished. I called the attention of the Minister of Public Works to this matter two years ago. At that time, if my memory serves me correctly, the minister said that it was his policy not to rent phones to anybody. [DOT]
Do any private companies operate in that part of the country?

Yes, but not in this particular section where the lines are to be built. My hon. friend challenged me to give instances of cases where Liberals were refused phones. I could give him a dozen instances. I challenge the-hon. gentleman to name one person in the district of North Inverness who is a Liberal and who has a phone. There is not one instance. I would no more use one of those phones if I had a political message to send than I would hang myself.

I challenge the hon.
gentleman to give names and places and to inform the committee where any Liberal has been discriminated against.
I will satisfy my hon. friend: North East Mairgaree and South West Margaree.
Give the names.

What are the rates
charged for a conversation over distances of 25, 50, 100 miles? There must he a certain schedule of tolls, according to the distance.

Does ith-e minister mean to tell the Committee that the Government puts up the poles and wines 'and establishes a telephone half a mile away from the main line for $4.50 a year? We bad better let the Government put in all the phones.

If I make a recommendation to the minister to give telephones to, say two or three persons in my district, will he give me an assurance that he will do so. I will give the minister my word of honour that I will recommend only persons qualified to use those telephones.

I have stated the policy
adopted by the department. As I understand it, if a man applies for a telephone along the line, the department gives it to him, and it is practically made a public telephone. Whatever the policy is-and that is as I understand it-if the hon. member sends me the name of a party, I will see that he is put on that telephone line. There will be no discrimination. Every man will have the same right on that line, irrespective of politics or anything else. If a man, whether in my hon. friend's constituency or in any other portion of Canada, makes an application for a telephone on a government line, I will guarantee that the policy of giving the public the use of those telephones as freely as it can be given will be carried out,

I notice in this report on telegraph statistics, which I have in my

hand, the gross revenue for 1916, on lines under the control of the Dominion Government, amounts to $181,227.04, while the expenses amount to $661,982.34. There is therefore, a very large deficit.
