There is a great difference between the revenue and the operating expenses.

I have listened for a long time to this discussion which seems to be more or less of a family quarrel amongst hon. members from Nova Scotia. I have never before seen the minister begged so hard to refrain from giving hon. gentlemen money as the minister has been begged today. I feel like voicing the opinions of my hon. friend (Sir Sam Hughes) and the hon. member for Renfrew (Mr. Graham) that this- is an opportune time to ask the minister to turn his eyes to Ontario, the people of which province want the service that the people of Nova Scotia apparently do not desire.
While I quite understand it is hard to strike out an item that has been inserted after mature deliberation on the part of tlie officials surely the 'minister can do so this afternoon after the heckling he has received from the hon. member for Guys-borough (Mr. Sinclair) who says:	I have
a number of friends who are going to get this extension, but, on their behalf, I do not want it and I ask you to strike out the item. The hon. member -for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) -wants to strike out everything. The hon. member for North Cape Breton*(Mr. McKenzie) would also become very economical and not let anything further get to his friends. The hon. -member for Inverness (Mr. Chisholm) is split in two; he is divided in the middle; he wants it and he do-es net want it; he says: If -a real Liberal can get on to the extension, so that he will not be overheard, I want it; if that cannot be done, I do not want it. It is all a question cf politics with hon. gentlemen opposite. I am sorry the hon. member for North Bruce (Mr. Hugh Clark) is not in the House. We have in old Ontario, to say nothing of the new, a large territory in which a system of this kind would be of great advantage. Take the Bruce peninsula, the land contiguous to Georgian bay and lake Huron, the territory running up to lake Nipissing and the north country; we can take thousands of miles of telegraph or telephone lines if the Government will only

give them to us. They would be of great benefit for life-saving purposes when storms occur on the lakes, and for warning against forest fires. These wants are apparently all- satisfied in Nova Scotia.

The people there do
not want them.

They have them and
they are using them. It is time for the Government to strike out those extensions which they have been coaxed to strike out. Why should the Government leave them in the estimates? Hon. gentlemen opposite represent the people there; they know what their constituents want, and they say those extensions are of no use to the electors, ratepayers, and citizens of various constituencies in Nova Scotia. Under the circumstances, I would for once go over the heads of the department who have recommended those public benefits and say to the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair): All right, we will cut out your extension telegraph service; and I would say the same to the hon. member for Inverness (Mr. Chisholm).
I am heartily in accord with the idea of continuing the ex-penditurey The hon. gentleman is wrong when he includes me with the other hon. members.

I will leave my hon.
friend to fight it out w-ith his fellow members on the other side. I take from his statement the argument that the extension is of some service in at least one county
Certainly it is.

-and that the extensions are desired and required. I would out out all the extensions except that one in the county of Inverness, on the request of the hon. members who represent those counties. The money could be saved and sent up to the province of Ontario, as extensions are very badly needed in some of the northern sections in which the inhabitants are labouring under greater disadvanages than are the people of Nova Scotia. If there is any legal way of, accomplishing this, the minister should strike out all those other extensions now and give extensions' in the northern parts of Ontario where they are much more needed.
Excepting Inverness.

The hon. member is
altogether wrong in saying that I oppose any accommodation to the people in my county of North Cape Breton and Victoria. The
wrong infcrmation was given to me by the minister. Inadvertently he told me he was going to put in three miles of telephone line at the end of about 100 miles of telegraph line. I could not understand the sense of putting in three miles of telephone line which would have no connection with any telephone system. After a little further inquiry, the minister and I discovered that this was merely a three-mile extension of the telegraph system in the county, and with that I am perfectly satisfied. I did however, combat the idea of building three miles of a telephone line all by itself with no earthly connection with any other telephone line and of no use to anybody. Those telegraph lines in the northern part of Victoria and throughout Cape Breton were put in by our own friends when we were in power, and we are not going to find fault with them to-day.
New Brunswick telegraph and telephone lines -Chatham-Escuminac and Point Sapin telephone line-extension to Kouchibouguac, $3,000.
The superintendent states that this extension is required in order to reach the fishery establishment at Kouehi-bouguac.
Who owns the fishery establishment?
The W. S. Loggie Company, Limited.

As I am afraid there may be some connection between the W. S. Loggie Co. Limited and the hon. member for Northumberland, I want to put myself straight on the situation. I am just as strongly opposed to this vote as I was to the vote in regard to Nova Scotia, or as I will be in regard to the votes in regard to Quebec and British Columbia. I have never been on the ground actually myself, but, as I understand, perhaps 30 or 40 years ago the Federal Government built a telegraph line from Chatham, down the south bank of the Miramiohi river, running out to a point at the mouth of the Miramichi river called Point Escuminac. This line was extended to Point Sapin. It was for many years run as a telegraph line, and no doubt was of very great value, because it was used in connection with shipping; the arrival and departure of vessels being telegraphed to Chatham and in that way reached headquarters at Ottawa. I have never been at this place myself and, therefore, I cannot speak with the knowledge of the toon, gentleman from Northumberland, but I know that the New Brunswick Tele-

phone Company goes to Escun^jpac, and has a line to Kouchibouguac. It seems this is a proposal to extend the line beyond the point at which the Government line of telephone comes in contact *with the 'New Brunswick line.
Do I understand that when this is constructed it will join up (the present Government system?

No, they are joined up now. Some years ago the telegraph line was converted into a telephone line, and an arrangement was made with the New Brunswick Telephone Company by which there was interchange of service. I do not remember the details, but I think it was satisfactory to both companies, as they come together at Kouchibouguac. This proposal is that the Government shall extend 10 or 12 miles further down the bay. I aim opposed to it.
Will there be opposition?

I trust the minister
will not treat too seriously the abuse which has been heaped on the Government telephone lines by hon. gentlemen opposite. I happen to know about that part of the line to which my hon. friend refers. It extends from Chatham to Point Sapin, part iu Northumberland county, and part in Kent county. It i's about 50 or GO miles in length, and the proposition is now t-*. extend it from Point Sapin to the Kouchibouguac river, following the shore, through districts spars-ley settled, and altogether out of communication with the rest of the world. The people who live along the shore are engaged in fishing and the telephone service is their only means of communication with the outside world. The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) referred to the New Brunswick Telephone Company, and the readiness of that company to do anything they could to give telephone facilities to the people of New Brunswick. I do not know how telephone companies act in other parts of the Dominion. But I want to say that in New Brunswick, so far as telephones are concerned, we have one of the worst monopolies in the Dominion of Canada. We formerly had two companies in New Brunswick, the Central 'Telephone Company and the New Brunswick Telephone Company. I do not know to which company the hon, gentleman belongs, but today competition has been absolutely abolished by the absorption of the Central Telephone Company by the New Brunswick Telephone Company. The hon. gentleman has stated that the New Brunswick Telephone Company was always ready to come to the rescue of people who desired telephone communication and I desire to say that that is not so. I know a number of irstances where applications were made to the New Brunswick Telephone Company to extend their lines to different localities

and They would n-ot give the people these facilities. The New Brunswick Telephone Company was generous enough to say to the people: You put up the poles, we will put up the wire, and the line will belong to us. That was the basis upon which they were prepared to give telephone communication to these people. The proposed line will end at Kouchibouguac beach. It does not connect in any way with the New Brunswick Telephone line at Kouchibouguac; it connects with the main line at Chatham, and gives very valuable service to the people of that section of the country; the government will be well advised, if they extend the system further whenever needed. Reference has been made to the amount paid for rental om these lines, and the $4.50 rate has been considered ridiculous by gentlemen opposite. Well, $4.50 at first sight is ridiculous, but it is not quite so ridiculous when you take into consideration the fact that by paying $4.50 you merely get communication with Chatham, and the localities along that line, which I say are sparsely settled.
60 miles of communication.

60 miles of communication through wilderness, and the New Brunswick Company would not, under any consideration, undertake to build the line there, and the moment you reach Chatham if you want to communicate with any other portion of the province you must pay 25 cents to the New Brunswick Telephone Company. If you were to telephone into Chatham, in order- to get your connection with the town of Chatham you must pay a pretty heavy toll. The Department of Public Works would be well advised not to pay too much consideration to all this howl which is raised against their telephone lines, which are giving good service to a portion of the population, which would not get any service at all were it not for those lines.

I do not want to go into a dissertation about the vices or virtues of this telephone company, because I would be very much out of order. I want to say to the hon. gentleman, however, and I am very glad to have an opportunity of making this statement to-day, that the New Brunswick Telephone Company has no monopoly in any portion of the province pf New Brunswick, Any person or any company who can get the rights from the municipal authorities is absolutely free to parallel the lines of the New Brunswick Telephone Company at any place. We have competition in many parts of the province, and we encourage the construction of local companies wherever we can. In many cases we hand over certain territory to those people and say:	Now, develop it.
When I hear of the trouble they are having in Ontario in regard to telephone companies, I think there must be something wrong, either with the Bell Telephone Company or with the local companies, because we have no friction whatever in the province of New Brunswick. My hon. friend speaks about the charges made. It may surprise him to learn that in the province of New Brunswick we have the cheapest telephone service in the Dominion, and we have the finest example in Canada of what can be done by a properly organized and properly conducted public utility corporation. We have no mortgages and no bonds, and a very small capitalization.
What does the farmer pay per year?
Fifteen dollars, for unlimited service.
A party line?

Unlimited party line
.service. In some of the towns we get the service down as low as $15. To show you the difference between a properly operated company-owned line and a government-owned line, I will give you an illustration. There are about 1,000 telephones in the town in which I live, about one-half in the town and one-half in the country-the country subscribers get the service for $15 a year, and I thin^ the lowest rate in the town is $15 or $18.
That is for house telephones?
Yes, $18 for a business telephone. I simply mention this to show what can be done when a company operates a public utility under proper conditions.

Why is it lower in some
towns than in others?

Because of the service given. The larger the exchange the higher the price, on the theory that they are getting more service from the telephones. So far as I know, the New Brunswick Telephone Company has never refused to grant a service, even though it be not upon a paying basis. No doubt there have been

many applications for service which have not been granted, and you will find that everywhere. My hon. friend says that if the people will erect the poles the company will agree to string the wires. That is- true in many cases, and it has frequently been taken advantage of. I presume the same thing applies all over Canada. I would like to ask my hon. friend from Kent (Mr. Robidoux) whether the New Brunswick Telephone Company was ever asked to construct the line in question under this vote.

I cannot give my hon. friend the information, but I believe the matter was broached when Mr. Richard O'Leary was a member of the board of directors of the New Brunswick Telephone Company, and my information is that the company could not consider the question of establishing a telephone line in that district, 'because the line would have to be built through about ten miles of uninhabited country, from which no revenue would 'be derived. From a business standpoint the proposition could not be considered at all, and the New Brunswick Telephone Company would not consider it. The company is not in business for the good of the health of its members; it is in business for dollars and cents, and that is the policy it followed ever since it has had the monopoly. Before the New Brunswick Telephone Company had obtained a practical monopoly in the province we could get certain privileges and certain advantages from the rival companies, but evidently the competition was not satisfactory to the shareholders of the New Brunswick Telephone Company, so they absorbed these other companies. This was good business. Although it is permissible for any man or any body of men to start a telephone company in the province of New Brunswick, it is a difficult matter to carry on a business of that kind with competition as strong as the competition of the New Brunswick Telephone Company. For that reason there are no rival companies. In many instances the rates of the New Brunswick Telephone Company are fair, but in many others which I could enumerate if this were the time and place, they are unfair.

If the Government persists in spending $272,000 to instal new lines, when $50,000 or $60,000 would 'be sufficient to repair the old lines, when they go to the people and ask them to economize, they need not be surprised if the people laugh at them and have no confidence in their sincerity. If they propose to build

new lines to the extent of at least $200,000 which could be done without until the war is over, and then ask the people to contribute for war purposes, they need not be surprised if the people ask them why they did not save $200,000 when they had an opportunity. I protest strongly against a dollar being expended for new lines at the present time. Old lines should be repaired and kept in as good conditions as possible, but the people of Canada can until after the war join in the sacrifice which is being made, by doing without telephone lines which they never before had. If the Government persists in spending this money at the present time, they are not keeping faith with the people, and they are not using their best endeavours to conserve the finances of the country in order that the war may be prosecuted.

I do not rise for the purpose of objecting to or criticising the particular item under discussion. I would like to ask the acting Minister of Public Works upon what basis he makes the estimate to give aid to certain sections of the province and not to the others? I quite understand the argument made by my hon. friend from Kent (Mr. Robidoux) that it would be a very great advantage if the Government owned the telephone service in that section of the province of New Brunswick which is sparsely populated. But there are other portions of New Brunswick to which the like argument would apply. Will the same consideration be granted to other portions of New Brunswick as is being granted to this section?

This is merely an extension of the present line. We are not adopting the policy of starting out in some other place to build an entirely new line. My hon. friend from South Renfrew is protesting against expenditures on account of war conditions. He is absolutely right and we all agree to that and we have curtailed expenditures. But, there are urgent cases like the present where the extension is to give communication to a large fishing industry. We are urging people to catch more fish and that large industry has increased its output for the benefit of the people during the war. No Government can sit still and not do what is necessary in connection with the works that are already established. Some hon. gentleman states that the Government system does not amount to much. We have some 10,000 miles of telegraph service throughout Canada while the Great Northwestern Telegraph Company has 10,000; the Canadian Pacific Railway Telegraph Com-

pany, 14,000 and the Grand Trunk Pacific
5,000.	We are in the business in about as large a way as any of them. The only difference is that the Government have to build these lines in sparsely settled districts where a private corporation would not extend their system. Would* the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) who is interested in a telephone company say that the Bell Telephone Company are not extending their line one mile during this war; hut that they are taking the money that they might use for extensions and putting it into war bonds?
Our company are certainly extending their lines the least possible distance and we are putting every dollar we can get our hands on into war bonds or into contributions to the Patriotic Fund.

The hon. gentleman has answered my question as I expected he would. He admits that they are extending their lines to the least possible extent and I tell him that the Government are doing the same, as was proved when the hon. member for Inverness complained that he had asked for 7j miles of telegraphic line and that the minister had cut it in two.

The minister talks about his great system of 10,000 miles of telegraph and telephone lines. This is a system that was started to reach parts of the country that could not possibly be reached by any ordinary business organization. They had to go to 'the Yukon, twelve or fourteen years ago and that takes in 1,000 miles. They had to go to Labrador to facilitate the navigation of the river St. Lawrence, and that takes in 2,000 or 3,000 miles, and they had to go down the north shore of the St. Lawrence for the same reason. Years ago they constructed a line from Chatham to Point Escuminac, which also was necessitated by the requirements of navigation. But that is a different principle altogether. That does not get you away from the fact that the hon. gentleman, on the eve of an election, is expending over a quarter of a million dollars for telephone lines that are not needed. Do you tell me that it is necessary for the industries of this country, for the carrying on of the war, or for the carrying on of the affairs of the country, that this Government should expend $3,000 to extend a little telephone line in the constituency of my hon. friend from Kent? It is a most wonderful thing how they have got along there for fifty or seventy-five years without a telephone line. It is a
most wonderful thing that any of the telephone companies in New Brunswick have not heard about this. It is a remarkable thing that they have carried on their business down there without a telephone line, and that just on the eve of an election my hon. friend wants to spend $3,000 in order that the hon. member for Kent may obtain a few votes. That is what we object to. Ii the Government telephone system were a real business proposition from which they were expected to pay interest on the investment it would be a different thing. But we know that these are not business propositions. We know that they never expect to get a cent of revenue from the investment. We have the admission that they spend $600,000 or $700,000 a year in getting a revenue amounting to about one-third of that. But what I am saying now is only a bagatelle as compared with what ought to be said with reference to some other items in the estimates. A man would not know very much about what was real loyalty to his country who would stand up without protesting against the proposal of the Government to launch out into the expenditure of this enormous amount of money simply that there might be easy sledding for certain of his friends when the election comes on.

The acting Minister of Public Works did not answer my question in regard to the policy of the Government. He made the statement that this amount was being expended in that section of the country for the purpose of reaching the fishing establishments and giving the people tele phonic communication with Chatham and elsewhere in Kent and Northumberland. Is it proposed to extend that system to any other localities in New Brunswick?
I know of farmers who have left their places because they could not get telephone connection. It is as important to farmers to have telephone communication as it is to fishermen, and if the policy laid down with regard to this line is right, it would be equally correct to give assistance to agricultural communities in the outlying settlements of the different provinces. If I can say to my constituents that the Government will assist them in establishing telephonic lines of communication with the more populous centres, they will consider it a great advantage. Leaving aside the general question of public ownership, I can see no reason why one section should get this advantage and assistance and other sections be denied it.
The policy of the Government is only to extend certain lines that are in existence, not to build new lines in new localities.
What is the difference between extending an old line ten miles into a new district and building ten miles of line in a new district?
The difference is that to adopt such a policy would involve a very large expenditure. These are small amounts to extend some of the present lines a few miles.
How many phones does the minister anticipate placing on this ten or twelve miles of line, and what will be the estimated cost and the revenue?
I shall have to get that information between now and eight o'clock.

Is this line to be operated on the same principle and under the same conditions as the line in Nova Scotia, which is that there will be no such thing as a man renting a phone, but that a phone will be placed in somebody's place of business or residence, and people will go in and pay a certain toll? I understand that this line will extend about 70 miles to Chatham. If this system is to be adopted, does it mean that the same charge will be made for all points on that 70 miles, and, if so, what will that rate be?
That is a very reasonable question and I shall procure the information before eight o'clock.

I may say that I am absolutely opposed to the whole system and feel like criticising each item and getting all possible information. I think it necessary that the people should have some of this information in order that they may realize what an awful system is being imposed on them for what, in my judgment, is purely a political reason. I shall continue to ask questions and I hope the minister will realize that I am doing it only from a sense of duty.

The information I have before me is what it is usual for the minister to have in passing these estimates, but of course there may be questions that call for fuller information and I shall have the proper official here at eight o'clock. It is better to have the items criticised because in that way information may be forthcoming which will be valuable to the minister in respect to either expenditure or opera-

tion. I want the hon. -member to feel that I am not withholding any information.

As the minister is in the happy position of not having any information, of course he cannot withhold it. If this discussion has done nothing but reveal the condition of affairs existing in the county of Inverness, and if it produces a remedy for that condition of affairs and places this system in such a position that it will not be an absolute political machine but will be of some benefit to the public, the afternoon will not have been spent in vain.

Mr. BOULAY- In making appropriations for telephone lines the Government has evidently forgotten a part of the country which is in great need of that service. I refer to that part of Quebec extending fro- Matane to Gaspe, along the south shore of the St. Lawrence. This part of the province is settled chiefly by fishermen, whose only communication during the winter is by telegraph.. In this district, which covers an area

of about 200 miles, lumber mills are being established and business is going to improve, but very likely the people there will never have the benefit of a railroad. Part of this district is in the county of Rimouski and part in the county of Gaspe. I hope the Government will bear my remarks in mind and make an appropriation next year with a view to improving the means of communication afforded to these people, who, as it were, are buried under the snow nearly seven months in the year. I think before we come to this we should have an explanation from the minister on what certainly is a new policy to a very great extent at least. I have before me a return which was brought down a few days ago containing a copy of the papers with reference to the Government of the Dominion building competing telephone lines in British Columbia paralleling lines of the Okanagan Telephone Company already in operation. Up to the present time the Government has been justifying the expenditure of those comparatively large amounts of money on the ground that the lines were being constructed in out-of-the-way districts, putting the people of those districts into communication with the rest of the world, and that it was impossible for such communication to be established unless the Government came to the rescue. I thought he strained it to the breaking point in dealing with the county of Dorchester. We all know conditions there, and the minister did not try to explain it at all. He simply threw himself on the mercy of the House and said. "For God's sake put this thing through." We have an entirely different condition of affairs in the province of British Columbia. The minister may say the idea is to give telephonic communication to outlying settlers, but before he does so I want to point out a few things which appear in this return, so that he will not stumble too far into it. We find there has been a genuine competition going on in the province of British Columbia between a well-established company, known as the Okanagan Telephone Company, and the Government. The

question was, which was going to win out. Of course the inevitable happened-the Government won out, because the Okanagan Telephone Company had to furnish their own money and run the line as a business proposition, and could not compete with the Government, which was throwing in money at the rate of $25,000 in the first year, and in 1915-16, $97,000, and it is now up to $200,000, and no man on earth could tell where it would be if things were unfortunately allowed to continue for three or four years longer. I find from the statement made 'by the local superintendent, Mr. W. H. Stevens, that the system of the Okanagan Telephone Company comprises about 138 miles, and consists of trunk lines built to connect nine local exchanges. These exchanges are located at Salmon Arm, Enderby, Armstrong, Vernon, Lumby, Kelowna, Peachland, Sunimerland and Penticton. The Government system comprises about 1,300 miles, and has been constructed for the purpos'e of affording telephone service to the widely-scattered settlements throughout the region, while incidentally operating six local exchanges located at Nicola, Merrit, Princeton, Hed-ley, Keremeos and Chase. Then there came a fight between Enderby and Vernon, I think, and in some cases for nearly 100 miles-I am not exactly sure as to the mileage, but for a long distance in any event-the Government lines and the company lines were parallel, and, as if that was not bad enough, the Government actually built another line parallel to the company line.
How long was that?
Somewhere about fifteen or twenty miles.
Is it not the other way? Did not the company build after the Government line?

No, the company built first and the Government line was built afterwards. It ran into 1916 and the matter was referred to the Minister of Agriculture. He took the very wise course of handing it back to the local superintendent. He said that the superintendent was on the ground and he knew the conditions better. But there was a recommendation by the Conservative Association. So they built the line. Finally it got so bad that they had to come to some kind of an agreement, and an agreement was entered into between the Government and the company. While I do not know the geography of that portion of

British Columbia sufficiently well to discuss it as the minister can, I think the great majority of these lines are in the minister's own constituency. I find here tens of thousands of dollars to be spent in the Okanagan country which I understand is in the minister's constituency. But here is one little thing that I can tell without being very intimately acquainted with the geography of the country. In the agreement between the parties it is provided that:
The company agrees to extend within three months the local circuit from Enderhy to Mara connecting with the Enderhy exchange to take care of the local business.
I find in these estimates this item:
Okanagan telephone system-establishment of rural system between Enderby and Mara, 52,100.
That must be the same thing. This carries out exactly the same idea as that laid down by the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue in Dorchester awhile ago in the House when he said: "The people want it." That is what is going on in British Columbia to-day. They made a trade with the Okanagan Telephone Company by which the telephone company is to do certain things; but sufficient political influence is brought to bear and the Government is doing it instead of the company.
When was that agreement entered into?
The 16th June, 1917.
These supplementary estimates were prepared some time ago and if that agreement was made since, of course, this item would not go on.
Well, if we knew these things we would discuss them.
When we come to the item we will strike it out.

The Minister of Agriculture has been for three or four years building up the Government telephone system in his county in competition with a private firm. Now he comes down to Parliament and asks for-and I suppose it will be forced through-a vote for $50,000 for building telephone lines. Why, he is worse than the Minister of Inland Revenue. That hon. gentleman only wanted a few miles. He is a poor innocent creature. The idea of the Minister of Agriculture entering into a conspiracy with the Minister of Inland Revenue and then beating him out to that extent-putting off the poor Minister of

Inland Revenue with a paltry $3,500 and taking $50,000 tor himself. The Minister of Agriculture must be covering every mount, crag and valley in his constituency with telephones. Then they jump over to Vancouver island. I suppose that is where our hon. friends from Vancouver island come in. I do not think they will contend that these are all extensions; they seem to be a lot of new works entirely. I realize that my hon. friends are all sitting around here, and I know that they are going to put up some plausible excuse for all this expenditure; but, after all, the only possible excuse is the election, nothing else in the World. These people know that without something like this they are in pretty bad shape in British Columbia, and they are simply calling upon the people in the eastern part of Canada to put up money to help them to win the election. I would think it pretty small business if the people in eastern Canada were playing the game that our friends from the West are playing. I suppose that nothing that anybody could say would divert the minister from carrying out the wishes of his friends, but this is opening up something which is very vicious. I do not know if you would expect it. There has been a good deal of talk about the Canadian Northern deal, but this is as bad as that-it is worse, because that is a great transportation proposition, it is in existence and it must be carried on in some way. Men may honestly differ as to the manner in which we should work out the Canadian Northern problem, but here is a new policy of spending public money which should be expended by the people of the locality, as is being done in nearly every other portion of Canada. All the telegraph and telephone lines which the Government have built heretofore, except in British Columbia, have been in outlying districts where there are very few people, but I learn by this report that they go into the city of Armstrong, and they are able to string their lines on electric light poles some sixty in number. Talk about going to the outlying districts. They find that traffic is so heavy that they are compelled to have additional facilities to enable them to carry on the business. Yet they say that it is necessary in order to give the people telephone communication. I think we ought to have some explanation of this matter from the minister. I am glad to see he is going to strike out one item. He should strike out the whole of those items excepting possibly that for the Yukon. I know nothing about that. I assume that,
if there is to be telephonic communication in the Yukon, it may be necessary that it should be provided by the Government. With that exception, I can see no justification for this expenditure excepting that it is necessary to get votes in the coming election.

I do not purpose taking up very much of the time of the committee but I do not want to allow the remarks of my hon. friend-although I think they are not meant seriously-to pass without saying a few words. He seems to think that there is something sinister and peculiar in the extension of the telephone system in British Columbia. A good many remarks have been made about the system in British Columbia, and I think that the committee, or some members of it, are under some misapprehension regarding the whole matter. My hon. friend said that I seemed determined to cover every crag, valley and mountain in British Columbia with telephones. When I tell the committee that my own constituency of Yale-Gari-boo is twice as big as the whole of the Maritime Provinces, hon. members will understand that we are dealing with a condition of things that is in no way comparable with the condition to be found in any other part of Canada. This telephone system has sprung out of the desire to give communication to the old established settlements far from civilization throughout the province, and as the traffic would not justify any company in taking it up it was only natural that the Government should do it. It was not this Government that took the step first.
For instance, in the north end, in 1904, when I first went over my present constituency, I took a team of horses at Ashcroft, leaving the main line of the Canadian Pacific and drove 755 miles before I saw the railway again. There were settlements like Barkerville into which gold miners went from California in 1862. These men are hundreds of miles away from other settlements, shut off from every one else. There were men there in 1904 who had never even seen a railway, some of the old miners who had gone in there in 1862. I think it is perfectly desirable and justifiable that such pioneers, who have settled the remote parts, should have, .even at the expense of some of the more fortunate parts of the country, some of the advantages of modern civilization, particularly in the way of communication. That all sounds very nice from the standpoint of a meniber who wants public money expended in his constituency, and I have no doubt that everything the hon. minister has said is true. We know that if people go out into the mountains a hundred miles from Ashcroft on the Caribou road they must not expect much civilization. But they have been going there for fifty or sixty years and people have got along very well. Perhaps they have suffered in many cases from want of telephone communication, and there is no doubt that the telephone will be as great a benefit to these people as has been pictured by the minister. But you do not have to picture tilings like that. I am surprised that my friend took up so much time telling us the benefits of telephone communication with the outside world. We all know as much about that as he does, although
10 p.m. we may not know as much about the internal conditions of British Columbia. But any one who has ever been there knows that the Lord never intended very many people to live there anyway, and he will not be disappointed in the next'one hundred years.

While my hon. friend
says that the Lord never intended many people to live there, down in the Okanagan valley, for which many of these votes are asked, they have sent-and that is only a very small part of my constituency-nearly
3,000	men to the front to fight our battles.

Yes, and they have sent them from all over Canada, too. It is no use of my friend trying to wave any flapdoodle flags. We are talking business tonight, and if my friend wants to get on his hind legs and talk that kind of thing vye will do it with him. But let us talk business now, and my friend can talk tomorrow on the other side of the case. He talks about sending 3,000 men from the Okanagan valley. Does he think that he is justified, under present conditions, in spending 8300,000 since the war began, in order to give telephone communication to his constituents? That is the question which I want him to answer. That is the ground on which I objected last night to the expenditure of a quarter of a million dollars in the constituency of the member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley); that is the ground on which we are finding fault with this whole transaction. My hon. friend talks about sending men to the war; yet he is willing to use $300,000 that ought to be devoted to taking care of these men and furnishing them with supplies and munitions. Where does my hon. friend get the $300,000?

Since the war began, taking into consideration this vote, the amount will be nearer $350,000 than $300,-000-that is for telephones alone in British Columbia. My hon. friend talks about sending men to the war; he had better try to get money to keep those men supplied with munitions. I was charged last evening with doing a mean thing when I tried to direct the attention of the Acting Minister of Public Works to the actual condition of financial affairs in Canada to-day. I doubt whether the members of this House really know how serious the financial conditions are. 1 know enough to make me feel that every man in Canada who has any desire to see Canada do its duty in this war must be very seriously concerned about our financial condition. If these were normal times and the Government were anxious to embark on the principle of public ownership of telephones, I know of no place in Canada where such services are more greatly needed than in British Columbia. But it is wrong to spend $300,000 to give my hon. friend's constituents telephone communication at a time when the money is needed so badly that I dare not say here how badly it really is needed. My hon. friend knows the conditions better than I do. These works may be called extensions, but after all they are new expenditures. The Government has taken over the Okanagan Telephone Company. The people in that country have got along all right for some years with the Okanagan Telephone Company and its connections; yet fifteen or twenty extensions are proposed from the Okanagan telephone line out into different parts of the country. It might be wise to engage in this work in times of peace, hut it is not all right in time of war, when undertaken by the Minister of Agriculture in order to get votes. At a time when the Empire is simply up against it in respect of the necessities of the war, the Minister of Agriculture presses the Minister of Public Works, against his will, to put a proposal like this through the House. I do not.think we had



better hear any more from the minister about the men that have gone to the front from his constituency.

I was not forced to apply for these votes. Many of them were not known to me; they were applied for by people interested who thought they were justified. My hon. friend showed unnecessary heat in regard to one of my remarks when he said that it was no wonder that few people settled in that part of British Columbia. I merely mentioned the number of enlistments as an indication of the number of the people there were in that particular valley.

My hon. friend says that he did not ask for the vote. I find by this correspondence

The minister had the
benefit of the advice of a gentleman who was very close to the gentleman who is sitting beside him (Mr. Stevens), and who,
I think, probably would know about the matter. The minister cannot take much credit to himself because he did not know of some of these items. I have no doubt that he knew about all of those affecting his own constituency.

These items are all in the estimates, and I would like them to pass. As the Minister of Agriculture has stated, we will let the department look over the whole matter again, and if there are any items that we can stand over I will promise the hon. member that, unless the works, are urgently required, we shall not go ahead with them.

As it is late in the season, we may not be able to go ahead with some of them. I will promise to keep the expenditure down to the very lowest possible point and to have the whole matter looked into again.

That is a fair proposition, although I observe by the returns of last year that work was carried on during November and December. There is a return by Mr. Stevens, the superintendent, that one man was in charge from the 3rd of October to the 12th of November, at which date another man took charge, and there is nothing to show how long lie

woiked, so the fact that it is late in the season would not make any difference. I pointed out the night before last how they can do these things when it is necessary and when there is an election coming on. Last February, in New Brunswick, they built roads when there was four feet of snow on the ground, and the people of that province do not know anything gs compared with the people of British Columbia in regard to matters of that kind. With this pledge from the minister, while I do not withdraw my opposition, I do not feel it is necessary for me to say anything further on this subject.

I must again bring to the notice of the department my serious ground for complaint about expenditures of this kind. I have repeated over and over again that my people will expect n*e to bring this matter to the attention of the ' minister. The people of my province have had large votes and large works promised to them. They have harbours requiring improvements, and fishermen of my province are in need of breakwaters and wharves. The gentleman who was for some years responsible Minister of Public Works, (Mr. Rogers) told us that the situation was grave; that money was required for other purposes, and that we must not press for money at all. As I have shown from Hansard to-night, we accepted his word in regard to the matter, and we stopped pressing for these appropriations. We were told that all the money the country could get together was for one purpose only; that any other expenditures would be of the slightest possible kind and only in regard to matters of the greatest possible urgency. The Minister of Agriculture has been in this Parliament as minister since 1911. In 1911, 1912, 1913 and the early part of 1914, there was an overflowing treasury. He found the -treasury with $40,000,000 of a surplus in it, with all bills paid and the country carrying splendid sail, and everything all right. But during those years from 1911, to 1916 there was nothing in the estimates about those telephones and telegraph lines in British Columbia. Conditions have not changed in regard to them since my hon. friend became Minister of Agriculture. The necessity was just as strong years ago as it is now, and I cannot understand why a minister of the Crown should come to us at this stage, a few weeks before an election, with an extraordinary presentment of this kind. I think I have been in this House longer than
the Minister of Agriculture, and in my experience of fourteen years I have never seen a private member or a minister taking the responsibility of presenting for the consideration of a committee of this House such an array of items as he presents to us in the midst of a war and a few weeks before an election. He had five or six years of better conditions when those things might have been presented, but not a word was said about them The minister may be acting in absolutely good faith, but, in view of the conditions confronting us, it looks as if this were done for a purpose, particularly in view of the statement by the ex-Minister of Public Works that no extraordinary expenditure of this kind would be made. All the ministers, who are supposed to be strong men in their counties, who are supposed not to require to be bolstered andi propped up by expenditures of this kind to ensure their return to Parliament, should set a good example of economy, and should run their 'elections upon their strength as men and as ministers and not float their elections on votes of this kind. If a private member should present to the minister a list of items for expenditures on behalf of his constituency, what answer could he make? No answer at all.

I wish to correct a statement which the Minister of Agriculture has made and which, I think, is an error. I do not say that he intentionally sought to mislead the committee, because I do not think the minister would intentionally mislead any one.
Certainly not.

The Minister of Agriculture rather put forward the argument that these extraordinary votes were required because the people to be accommodated were in remote settlements in British Columbia shut out from the world, and that, therefore, it was only reasonable and fair that they should have telephonic communication. But the larger amounts are for telephonic communication in well-settled districts of British Columbia. Take for instance the Golden-Windermere line, the extension from Windermere to Fairmont. There is a daily train running all the way from Golden to the Crow's Nest line, as my hon. friend knows. The country is well settled and there are quite a number of prosperous villages, almost towns, in that locality. It is one of the most beautiful sections of country to be found in the world, and a private telephone

system would be almost as apt to pay there as in any other -part of Canada. Then again take the Okanagan valley. There are some eight or ten telephone lines there connected with the Okanagan Valley Telephone system. There is a railway from Sicamous Junction to the head of the lake, and there is daily steamer communication, summer and winter, from the head of the lake to the foot. The country is beautiful, rich and well-settled. That surely does not come within the description that the minister has sought to give to the committee of the localities occupied by those people to whom telephone accommodation is being given. Let us take the largest amount in the estimates, $28,000 for an extension from Ashcroft to Agassiz in connection with the Okanagan Valley Telephone system. Both of those points are stations on the Canadian Pacific. Thus the proposal is to spend $28,000 to build a telephone line between two important stations on that line of railway.
They have the Canadian Northern on the other side of it.
It cannot be said that the people in that district are shut out from the world. They have the two termini, and the stations on the Canadian Pacific.

My hon. friend shows he is unacquainted with the facts. The item he has mentioned, $28,000, was put in the estimates, I believe, on the strongest possible recommendation of the Board of Trade of Vancouver.
Yes.

For this reason: hitherto the only telephonic communication between the large mining centres of the interior of British Columbia and the coast, the financial centres, has been Seattle, Spokane, and north from Nelson and further in. It has been an exceedingly difficult method of communication. By linking the line from Agassiz to Ashcroft, we can have a direct line through from the coast to the interior. One of the great trials in British Columbia during the 25 years that I have been a resident of the province has been to see millions and millions of dollars worth of business going to Spokane every year from the interior of British Columbia. Two things are going to overcome that. One is already in operation, the Kettle Valley railroad. That is one of the most necessary works to link up the coast district with the interior. This telephone system is another vastly important one. My hon. friend from Carle-ton (Mr. Carvell) mentioned another thing,

and that is the necessity for retrenching, because of economic conditions. I do not want to make any far-fetched argument. I am discussing this matter from a business and economic standpoint. We have been developing in British Columbia certain mining centres. We have Princeton and we have Hedley, and we have mining districts on the Kootenay further east again. These have all been linked up by the Government system, and they would never have been linked up by any other system. A great many of these items, while headed Okana; gan, have very little to do with the settlement of Okanagan. They connect the main Okanagan trunk line with outlying districts and with centres remote from civilization. The mining centres are usually away off in the mountains, remote from settled districts.
I will give one illustration, to give the committee an idea of what we are up against. One company has spent about $3,000,000 in the last two years in diamond drill work at Copper mountain. They have actually proven that there is over 11,000,000 tons of copper ore in the mountain, and they are tunnelling to take it out. That is only one company, and there are dozens. One of the greatest industries is mining, and the only way you can successfully produce from bur mining resources is by having adequate communication and proper methods. Those are essential.
How far is that mine from the main Government line?	j
I should say it would be about ten miles.

And that company. has spent $3,000,000 in drill work, and want the Government to provide them with a telephone? In New Brunswick the lumbermen would have provided themselves with a telephone, if they spent a fraction of that sum.

I say that is just an illustration of what one company is doing, and we have dozens in the interior in a similar position. As far as telephonic communication is concerned, nearly all that mining business has been done through Spokane. My hon. friend will see'on the file letters from the Vancouver Board of Trade, which have been working on this proposition for years, to try and induce the Government to put this line through. The telephone company out there, which operates on the coast, goes to Agassiz; it would not build the line from Agassiz to Ashcroft and into the interior. No com-

puny would do that. There is a stretch of country there which, if we can connect it up, will bring the whole business of the interior of British Columbia into Vancouver, and it is of vital importance, not only to Vancouver but to Canada as a whole, to keep the business as far as possible within Canadian channels. When 1 went to British Columbia we used to think the dr-y belt south of Kamloops was utterly useless except for gracing. I do not think that at that time there was a bushel of wheat exported from that district. Last year 250,000 bushels was exported from Kamloops, raised in the district to the south, to which it is desired to extend this telephone line. I received a letter yesterday from a man who had gune in there, taken up land and gone into farming, and he said the only way to induce people to go into these districts was to give them some sort of communication. Then there is the Okanagan valley, which exported to different parts of Canada, over
3,000	carloads of fruit and vegetables. The hon. gentleman must remember that if you are going to develop production in British Columbia, or anywhere else, you have to provide facilities. Unfortunately in British Columbia our agricultural land is in the valleys, and is split up by long ranges of mountains, more or less remote, and can only be reached by certain avenues of communication. These votes are for the purpose of linking up the scattered districts in British Columbia. I know my hon. friend is not serious when he casts a reflection on British Columbia as a desirable place in which to live, as I know when he was there two years ago he expressed considerable pleasure over his visit. We will not censure him in that regard, because I am sure he does not wish to reflect upon the province. Those who have lived there for many years think a great deal of British Columbia as a place to live in.

The old saying, "Every [DOT] man to his liking, as the old woman said when she kissed the cow," but if it suits my hon. friend I have no objection. However, the hon. gentleman has made the strongest argument against the granting of this money that could possibly be made. Tie is speaking of a country where the mining companies are spending $3,000,000 . in development, and taking out $10,000,000 worth of ore. They have a valley which exports 3,000 carloads of fruit. The country around Kamloops which was always supposed to be a dry country, last year exported a million bushels of wheat. In
our country, when we have conditions of that kind, we build our own telephone lines, we do not ask the Government to build them. No argument so absolutely condemns the proposition as that of my hon. friend from Vancouver.

The dredge was wrecked on the eoast of my constituency. The hawser broke, the dredge went on the rocks, there was no lifeboat and no way of the men escaping. I do not think we have had any information beyond that which has appeared in the newspapers.

There was an official examination by the wreck commissioner and the report is in the department. I have not got it here now. I am told that the wreck commissioner exonerates the officials of the Public Works Department entirely.
Who was to blame?
It was the storm. It was an extraordinary storm.
Why was the dredge sent there in the winter time?

She had gone before over the same course exactly in the winter time and no trouble had resulted. But in this case a great storm came on. The wreck commissioner, if any blame could be attached to anybody, would have had no hesitation in placing the blame.

My recollection is that a tug was taking this dredge along the' coast and that the men on the dredge were those who were drowned. They had no life-boats and no means of escape. Because of a defective hawser, the dredge parted from the tug and was swept on the rocks. I do not know how everybody can be exonerated from blame for an occurrence like that. I have never seen- any satisfactory explanation as to why that dredge was moved from one part of Nova Scotia to the other at that season of the year. There was no work for it at the place where it was going, and it was not sent there, I understand to do any particular work at that time. There is a suspicion among the people who have suffered from this accident that somebody was to blame.

If there had been any possible chance of blame being attached to anybody, the wreck commissioner would have found some one to blame. But be exonerates the officials in every way. In the report I find it is stated that:
The court found that the loss of the dredge and scows was due primarily to the scow breaking adrift from the dredge; secondly, the Roebling's hawser parting; and lastly, to the inability of the crew of the dredge to get the Roebling's hawser on board the scow. The loss of the crew is attributed to the fact that they did not get in. their boats when they were first put in the water, and why they did not do so, the court failed to understand.
No blame was in any way attached to the department in connection with the loss of the dredge.

In the meantime the captain of the Lisgar when he saw that the dredge had broken/ adrift attempted to heave his line in, which he could not do and then gave orders to cut the line. When this was done he proceeded close to the dredge in order to render any assistance possible.

The cable between the Magdalen Islands and the mainland lands at a place called Meat cove. On that account, for a time the winter news of which the hon. member (Mr. Lemieux) speaks was not conveyed from the mainland to the Magdalen islands. But the real reason was that the highly competent operator who had been in charge of the cable station at Bay St. Lawrence was dismissed by this Government. During the fifteen years that I represented Magdalen islands as part of the county of Gaspe, it frequently happened that the cable broke, because it is exposed to the shifting of the ice in that section of the gulf of St. Lawrence. Possibly that was the cause of the breaking in this instance.
As to the facts, I do not know. I know that the people of the Magdalen islands were given, during the. winter months, a synopsis of the news, and besides they had made arrangements with the Public Works Department through Mr. Keely, as they do most of their business with Halifax, Sydney, Pictou, and Nova Scotia generally, to wire their letters at a very low rate to the operator at Meat cove, and then the operator vvould^m.ail their messages to the firms at Halifax, Sydney or Pictou, thus facilitating business with the Magdalen islands during the winter months. I saw the hon. gentleman from Laprairie, who was called away, and he maintains the objection he made last night. I know the conditions because I was brought up in that district. which plied between Montreal and Laprairie was destroyed by fire seven or eight years ago, and you can see the remains of the steamer near the wharf, and the cham-nel which was used by that steamboat from Montreal to Laprairie has been partly filled, so that even if you were to repair the wharf, which is not badly in need of repair, you would have to dig a new channel between Montreal and - Laprairie for that size o.' boat.
I am striking it out.
It is not necessary.

There was the other item for Three Rivers, to which my hon. friend (Mr. Bureau) raised some objection last night. Last year we had an appropriation of $20,000 to repair this wharf, which is used on a large scale for the unloading of coal. The officials tell me it is absolutely necessary to finish up this work, and I would not feel justified in dropping the item altogether. I will have to ask the committee to allow it to stand.

Still you have the objection made by the hon. member from Three Rivers, which seems to be very radical. He said last night:
An additional amount was voted to complete the work, and it seems to he in perfect shape now. It was filled up with quicksand. That was washed out and it was refilled, branches, dirt and sand being put on the top. I do not see where the work is now required. They have been putting stone on the end of the wharf that faces the current and that meets the ice jams in the spring.
Considering the view taken by the hon. member from Three Rivers, who has a perfect knowledge of the situation, I do not see how the minister would be justified in maintaining that item.
I hardly think the hon. member for Three Rivers went into the matter as thoroughly as he should have done.

Will the minister promise in this ease, as he did in the case of the telephone lines, that before spending the money he will see that a proper inspection is made, and that no money will be spent unless it is absolutely required.
Mr. .REID: I will certainly do so.
New Brunswick-St. John harbour-extension of and repairs from Negro Point breakwater, $250,000.

Would the minister
state what the work would cost?

The work if proceeded with
would cost $750,000 to complete. We will

have to look into the matter thoroughly. In the meantime I would like the item to stand.

Are the figures based
upon the idea of utilizing stone from Partridge island?

The parties tendering were
free to take the stone from wherever they wished.
Ontario-Stayner-public building, $10,000.

I believe the minister
was going to consider the advisability of striking out this item. I think he should be guided by the fact that when the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) was asking for the passage of the Bill relating to taxation, and indeed in bringing forward subsequent measures, ne gave his assurance to the House that no new work would be undertaken. I think that pledge should be lived up to. A great many items have been struck out on that ground.

I agree that that was the
understanding, and therefore I am not sure that we will go on with the work.

I think it would be
better if the item were struck out.
Perhaps it would be ns well to leave it in, and we will not proceed with it if it is new work.

It must be new work,
because the amount is required to buy the land.
Mr. REID.- If that be so, I suppose we will have to strike it out.
The fact of it being there _is evidently a printer's error.

That is a very worthy
building, and it happens to be in a good Liberal town.
Mr. PUGSLEY': The building is only imaginary as yet.

Of course, if my friends
on the opposite side of the House want the item struck out, it cannot be helped.
What county is Stayner in?
It is the town of Stayner, which has done a lot for the war, and has never had a cent spent on it. in its whole history. I think it is only right that the town should be recognized.
Let it wait until we have a union government.
If we have a union government, of course the work will go on.

Are they all Liberals
there?

As a matter of fact there is no truce now, as there was when the statement was made that no new building would be proceeded with. When that statement was made there was a political truce between the parties, but the situation is changed now. The Opposition has forced the Government to go to the country, and I do not see why it is absolutely necessary that the arrangement made then should be carried out. During the last two days I have heard) nothing but abuse of the Government. Not a single item in the supplementary estimates passed without some blame being imputed to the Government. It was claimed the items were for a wartime election. If I had been the Minister of Public Works, I would have given a wartime supplementary estimate to hon. gentlemen opposite, and give them some excuse for kicking.
We think you would.

So did the hon. gentleman and there is no better politician or party man in this House than himself. As far as this public building in Stayner ,1s concerned, if hon. gentlemen opposite arc opposed to it, if they w'ant it struck ouf and if there is any agreement to firike on*, we will strike it out and let them take the blame.
St. John harbour-extension of and repaii-s to Negro Point breakwater, $250,000.

This is the only item of the Public Works Department left. I cannot add anything to what I said except that the work will cost probably between $750,000 and $1,000,000 before it is completed. This is asked for the commencement of the work and so much will be spent per annum. I would suggest letting the item go through, and of course we would have to consider going on with the work in view of the statements which have been made by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) and the hon. member for Carleton (Air. Car-vell). If the committee desire further information I will let the item stand.

If there is anything in the argument that no new work should be undertaken during war time, it is unfair to strike out the item of $10,000 for Stayner and then ask to have a quarter of a million dollar item left in as hon. gentlemen opposite are asking.
No.

The hon. member for St. John is well known to be very friendly towards this item. This is new work and it is not needed at all. It can very well stand over during the war, and I think the minister should strike the item out. There is no argument in favour of it that I can see as far as the rest of the country is concerned.
We will let the item stand.
I will be right here to fight it the next time it comes up.

I am not here to fight for St. John-it can take care of itself-bat there seems to be an argument in favour of leaving it in. The minister tells us that he has to call for tenders and that he is likely to accept one.
I have not accepted any. Tenders were called for but no action was taken.
How many were received5
It is not usual to ask. for tenders and then strike out the item.
Six regular tenders and four irregular.
Irregular In what way?

We required a certified
cheque with each tender, and no cheques were sent. Those that -were irregular were considerably higher than the lowest tender that was regular. I can say that the lowest tender is not that of a New Brunswick firm.
Why do you not tell us all about them and who they are?

I would not have any objection except that I have just got a memorandum now from the deputy and the tenders have not been submitted to council. It is not customary to give information about a matter of this kind until it has been submitted to council.

If the item is to stand over for a day or two I would be agreeable, but -otherwise I would like to present some very strong reasons for passing the item. This is a revote. The item was voted by Parliament two years ago and tenders were called by the minister for this work which was deemed very necessary and apparently essential for the protection of the harbour. Owing to the lowest tender being higher than the amount the minister thought he ought to expend,
he decided to call for new tenders. New tenders were called for under the previous vote. This is really a revote. .

Will the hon. gentleman tell me why it is not mentioned here that it is a revote? It says:
Extension of and repairs to Negro Point breakwater, $250,000.-
I do not know; but my hon. friend will find that what I say is true. It may be that tenders were called for to be paid out of the general vote for St. John harbour.
Yes, that is the reason.

I understand it was decided to make a change in the kind of stone that might be used. The previous tenders required that granite only should be used in the breakwater. A change was made in the hope that the tenders would be for a considerably lower amount. But, undoubtedly the vote in Parliament two years ago authorized the calling for tenders. The reason the work was not gone on with before was the belief that by .making this change it would be done at a lower cost.

I am willing that the item should stand, but I do not go back on what I said last evening. This is a new work in my judgment and I want to be fairly consistent. I opposed the rest of the new works and I oppose this.
What is the use of allowing this item to stand if we will not embark upon any new work?
The reason I ask that it be allowed to stand instead of striking it out is that I am only acting for the department and I would like to submit it to my colleagues.

It seems to be agreed that, the Minister of Finance having made that announcement, the committee is bound by it. I agree with my hon. friend' from North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) .that Stayner and St. John ought to be treated alike. I am prepared to vote to strike that item out.

I sincerely trust that the most my hon. friends wrould ask would be that the matter should stand a day or two so that it can be looked into. It is not a new work in the ordinary sense. The breakwater has been extended out from Negro point comparatively close to Partridge island. The department has done a lot of work, has built wharves, and the

opinion of experts is that the closing of this gap is necessary to protect the wharves and also the very large amount of shipping that is coming to the harbour and using these wharves on the western side. Therefore, this is simply carrying on a work which lias been in progress for a number of years.

My reason for asking it to stand is this: Tenders have been called for, they are in the department and I would not like to dispose of the matter without consulting my colleagues. We might allow the whole item to stand and I will bring it up when members are present without taking any advantage or asking it to be passed in their absence.

The hon. member for St. John wants to knock out a $10,000 item in Ontario, but he objects to the leaving out of an item for a quarter of a million dollars of which Ontario pays a large proportion. One item should stand against the other.

I would not do any injustice to any part of Ontario, or any other portion of Canada, but in the case of this building I have no doubt the post office is being carried on in rented premises. The land has not been purchased. The report says that the vote is required to purchase the land. The ex-Minister of Public Works last session dropped similar items with respect to public buildings and made the announcement that no public building would be undertaken while the war lasts.

Hundreds of thousands
of dollars needed to repair docks and improve harbours in Ontario, but there has not been a dollar of new work put in. This condition at St. John has existed from time immemorial.
No.

There is no condition there that requires any change, and we could go on for three or four years more without having this work done. I quite agree with the hon. member that this is new work, and hy what means of hocus-pocus that big item of a quarter of a million dollars can be put in these estimates, and even before it appears in the estimates tenders can be called for, is, I fancy, something entirely new in this department. This item is not urgent, and I think if one item stands the other should stand. If it is any money to be spent at St. John the late minister stands up for it, but he spends the time of this

House trying to stick his knife into . the items of other provinces, and I think it is time he was called in that respect-because if the rule is to be applied it should be applied all round. If it is a good rule, I am willing to abide by it; but let the hon. member for St. John abide by it and take the advice of his own colleagues and ask the minister to strike the item out.
My hon. friend is labouring under a very grave misapprehension. I did not try to stick a knife into-
You are, all the time.

I never did that. On the contrary, when I was minister and since that time, I have always encouraged development in all parts of Canada. See what has been done in the hon. member's own constituency, at Collingwood, and all through western Ontario. Very important works were constructed. I would appeal to representatives from these sections of Ontario as to whether or not I showed a generous spirit, not a niggardly spirit, in regard to improvements. The hon. member seems to think that conditions in St. John are what they have been for many years. That is not so. There has been a very large degree of harbour development there; a great deal of dredging has been done, and the wharves have been built lower down the harbour and nearer to the gap from which the southwesterly'storms affect the harbour, and it becomes, so these experts say, necessary to protect-
What experts?

The enginers and people connected with the harbour, experts of the department. There is a vast deal of shipping coming to St. John. It would amaze the hon. member to know what is being shipped to Great Britain, largely munitions and supplies for the Allies. Many vessels with cargoes of enormous value sail from the harbour, and those familiar with the harbour assert that it is necessary to fill up the gap in order to protect the shipping now coming in such great quantities to the harbour, and also that it is necessary to protect the wharves upon which a large amount has been expended by the Government.

I think the whole item looks very suspicious. For that reason I think the best thing we can do is to strike it out altogether.
